After twenty-five years of remarkable popularity, " The Private Secretarv.'" is, like another • famous comedy, " still running,;' and it has all the freshness imd power to amuse of its earlier t days. The great Briti,h public laughs as heartily as of yore while the portly Ir. Cattermole laboriously spells out his euphonious name and the innocent and long uffeting Rev. Robert Spalding, who does not like London, passes out of one serape into another. Large audiences have taken the opportunity of renewing their acquaintance with the old favourite at the Royal 'Court Theatre this week and they have been captured by the irresistible gaiety of the performances of Mr. Eugene C. Stafford's talented company. All the .artistes thoroughly enter into the spi it of their respective parts, and everything goes right merrily throughout the three acts. Mr. W. Hargreaves is to be credited with a distinct triumph as Mr. Cattermole. He is the life and soul of the .piece and when it is stated that he has portrayed the irascible old uncle from India no fewer than 7,000 times it is not sur- prising that he appears to live the pal t. He is seen at hfs best when he first makes the acquaintance of the uneffending cleric, whom he imagines to he his nephew, and the audience rocked with merriment when he prodded the Rev. Robert in the ribs, plied him with questions abcut his liver, and generally gave him a most unhappy time. Mr. Geoffrey Guise is also highly entertaining as the Rev. Robert Spalding, the embodi- ment of meekness and effiminacy, and we could hardly imagine abetter study of this character which is one of the most laughable and famous in the whole range of coa.edy. Mr; Frederick Tyrrell impersonates Mr. Sydney Gibson, the gentleman tailor, to the life, and he is especially clever in the scene when that worthy lapses from his usual high standard Of deport- ment under the influence of the flowing bowl. Mr. Arthur Claremont adds much to the gaiety of the evening as the high-spitited Douglas Cattermole, and he is especially. good while u:asquerading as the private 'secretary. He is well hacked up by Mr. Stewart Quartermayne (Harry Marsland). Miss Janice Deane. and Miss Lilith Gabriel, as Edith Marsland and her friend, are a vivacious pair and prove general favourites. Miss Evangeline Hope is most amusing as Mrs. .Stead, Douglas's much harrassed landlady, and Mrs. Alfred Davis gives a capital presentment of Miss Ashford, the devotee of spiritualism. 'The Private Secretary 7 is preceded by a one-act farce "The Wild man from Borneo,"which is decidedly lively and up-to-date. The orchestra, under Mr. Norman Lathara's baton. enlivens the intervals with some pleasing selections, including a tuneful valse "Fortuna, ' composed by the Rev. L. J. T. Daman, vicar of Walton. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. "MISS HOOK OF HOLLAND."

For next u kat the Royal Court Theatre- War- rington. the management have 'much pleasure in announcing "Miss Hook of Holland "direct from the ,Prince of Wales Theatre, London. The piece which made such a tremendous succe:-... in London is pre- sented by Mr. George Dance's talented Company. The music is the most fascinating feature of the play, and :the. plot as is usual in 'productions of this character, is just sufficiently strong to hold the interest of the audience. Miss Gertrude Melville will appear in the leaditig role or _Miss Sally Hook; the daughter of a wealthy liquer distiller, who, with his daughter's collaboration, makes up a blend of 01 different brews. Sally falls in love with a bandmastey (impersonated by Mr. Chas. Catley), who retirats her affection. She is loved also by Capt. Poop (Mr. Wood Massey), the bandmaster's superior officer). Old Hook who will be represented by Mr. Tom A.. Shale (of" 'Sergeant Brue " popularity), loses the famous recipe for his brew, and the same being found by-a street loafer, Simon Shinks (11r. Chas. E. Paton), is sold by the latter to the captain with the suggestion that it might avail him in furthering his love affairs. Before the finale, how- ever, Sally throws in her lot with the bandmaster, while the captain wisely transfers his affections. Paul A. Ruben's simple but effective . story of the land of dykes, cheeses, and schappes, combined with •the many delightful musical numbers from a pen of a gifted and vers.,atile composer, and the .quaint dresses • and scenery, make-up a captivating performance.

CHAPTER I.
The littl3 dried-up r_lan at V. 1.? ez•.(l of the table stood with his. glaz3s rai3,2d in his hand, gazing down the Lath of it at tile young man with the smiling, content-2d fv.ce.

" Mine is at once a plersing and a sate- factory duty to perform," said .the little dried-up man, clipping _his words carefully and precisely. " I introduce :y-oung John Baxendale into the Loire of-the Ilaxendales. From a legal pent of view I malze him free of them. He ct,mes to-day into hie kingdom." The old man cleared his throat, and paused for a moralut as if to consider his next wordi. The smiling guests about the table glanced at the young man at the end of it, and nodded at him in a friendly fashion, as thouzli tell- ing him that from an •ordinary human point of view he had very little to wish for in this viorld that he did net already pf ESeSS. "As you probably aircady know, mv friends," went en the precise voine, "young John Baxendale cornss of ag2 to-day, because he is five-and-twenty years old. That is to say, he comes of age in the legal sense, ac- cording to his father's will. On that we have to congratulate, him. But .I am given to understand "—the little dried-up man's eyes twinkled for a moment in 'quite an unaccus- tomed .way—" I believe we are all given to understand that be is not only a ltappy man in that sense, but in another. He is young— he is rich—and he is engaged to be married to one of the most charming- girls it has ever been my good fortune to meet. And lam an old man who, in my. time, has met many ladies of several generations. I see my young friend, Miss Evelyn, blushing. But she has nothing to blush about, save in the way of coming happiness. I ask you to charge your glasses, ladies and gentlemen, and to drink. to the health and the continued prosperity and happiness of Mr. John Baxendale !"

There were eoilfused eriee of Eaxenaale," "John," "Dear old John," and others 'of a like nature, as the guests sprang- to their feet with a rustling of dresses and the movement of chairs. John Baxendale sat still, with a flush upon his face, as he bowed to right and to left; then the people rustled back into their seats. The young man got to his feet slowly, and, at the storm of applause that greeted him, held up a protesting hand, and laughed. "My old friend, Mr. Goode, has said many nice things about me—some of them net quite true, I'm afraid," be began, in his sincere, boyish voice. "But he's said one thing that's true enough—and that was when be referred Ao my luck. If ever a man started- well in this world, on his twenty-fifth birthday, John 'Baxendale so starts to-nil.-r.ht. I assure you. IN haven't a care in the World, and I have every reason to believe ttat I am going to be a very happy man "7 —he glanced at the girl at one side of the table as he spoke, and for a moment her blue eyes met his with confidence —" and I know that I'm surrounded by some of the best friends ever a man bad in this world. My father—l raise my glass to his memory—was one of the best men that ever lived, and he saw to it that life was madi smoother for me than for most men of my age. From the bottom of my heart I thank you—as well for myself as for the dear girl who is to be my wife."

He sat down amid another murmur of ap- plause, and conversation became • general among the gueats. It Wrll6 evident that he was a great favourite. When presently the ladies rose to go to the drawing-room the men clustered about him, clapping him on the shoulder, and congratulating him over again on his good fortune. One man in par- ticular—a young fellow with a round, good. natured face, and. with a body somewhat in- clined to stoutness—linked an arm aff§C- tionately in that of John Baxendale, and woke almost enviously. "My dear John," he said, with a Intign. "I don't believe the.re was ever anyone born in this wor,d with a laxgecsilverepoon in hi i a mouth .than you. Which s no reflection on your mouth, dear bey—which is all that it should be—but is only a reference to your extraordinary geod fortune. Look at me—a penniless wretch that has to work hard for a living, when work is the last thing that I de- sire To do at all." _ _ _

" Ah, my dear Dick, the luck may not always last,- you know," said John Baxon- dale, with a note of seriousness in his tones. "There's always some sorrow in the world for eich one of us—and I expect I shall get my share in time." Don't croak ! " exclaimed Dick Munby, with a laugh, as he turned away. "There may -be some truth in that, John, after all," broke in the thin voice of. Mr. Felix Goode .at Baxendale's elbow. "There's always something in the background—some sorrow, or some conflict, of which we don't think at such a moment as this. Dot what" ever sorrow may come to you, you'll be ready to meet it, and to fight it—eh, John?" "I hope so," said the young man, lightly. "And- I'll wager it won't be very hea'vy—no- thing te frighlen a man. Shall we join the ladies?"

In the -great drawing-room John Baxeralale found himself, as by instinct, standing with Evelyn Kaylor. For an instant their hands met in that happy, secret fashion lovers un- derstand so-well. As they stood there, whis- pering, more than one pair of eyes was turned in their direction—to note the fair Saxon manliness of John, and the slim, dark beauty of the girl. Their whispers were for each other, and reached no other ears... "You're quite happy, Jack?" "So happy, my darling, that I'm a little afraid," he replied, with a laugh. "If such a thing were possible, I should say, like the old country folk, that ther was someolle walking over my grave.. Oh, don't look alarmed! I'm quite well, I assure you. Only I have a sort of uneasy feeling that perhaps this great prosperity of mine may not last— perhaps my happiness may change to sorrow." " You mustn't say that," she pleaded, twin- ing her slim fingers into his. " What should harm you? What should come into your life, or into mine, to spoil them? If we were poor to-morrow—if our friends 'fell away from 136, one and all, we‘should still have each other, shouldn't we?"
" Yes, thank He ! " he respende,tl. fer- vently. "We should always have each oth.2r."

There were only a few intimate friends at that birthday celebration dinner at Baxen- dale Hall. Baxendale Hall lies not far from the sleepy little town of Deepington, in the pleasant county of Susaex, and it has been in the possession of the Baxendales for several hundreds of years, as the old zlortraits in a great gallery upstairs testify.

It was a hot night in summer, and the win- dows leading from the great drawing-room to the terrace stood wide open. Within the room Evelyn was '.singing, and the man who was to_be her husband in the happy tine that W5B approaching stood outside on the terrace, looking out over the grounds, and thinking how, in the years to come, life was to go CA, smoothly for him here, with Evelyn's vnice to make the music of it. He was scarcey conscious of the fact that the voice presently aigul R.w.v: in fact, he only woke from his aream wnen ire gut Li:a Ler ni.s;:a on ro3 arm, and spoke softly. "Jack dear, what are ou dreamh about?" she Diked.

He started, and looked round at her; then once again fixed his iey,as- upon a certain- point among the trees. "I scarcely know what I was dreaming of," be repli,?.d. "I want you .to at the ei t which I am looking now—down there where thrse three great trees stand ch-,,5.e. toirer. There! did you see anything move then?" SLe wao silent for a ricmEnt ; then she seemed to catch her bre;_th tvaickly. "Yes. I -certainly saw a shadow dart' acrces there as you spoke," she whismersd. "Wait here until I come back. I'm coirg:

to see. WllO It 1:5, nor. • • -• • "But, Jack, it's cnin one of tin, aarvants or a gamekeeper," she u'-el. "Servants would noi. e onnd this side of 'ate house at this hon.a—nor waauld game- . keeDers." he renliad. A 3 he said the worda he stepped quiclAy do7.n from the terrace ; and plunged into the grounds. She waited for what seemed a .long time. She heard the murmur ot voices in the room, and cues a quick, high laugh. Then John Baxendale stepped again on to the terrace, and stcod there close beside her, lot-.;kir- out over the grounds with a perplexed fro‘:n. "I could have sworn I saw a man there— dodging about among the trees," he said, slowly, half to " I didn't want to call out to him, lest I might alarm you-, and he was gone so suddenly that I almost felt I might have been mistaken. I've- haif a mind to summon zorne of the men, and have the grounds searched," he added. • " I wouldn't trouble,'' she said. "The place is well guarded-and he's not likely to pass the dogs, whoever he is." " The dogs are pretty resLless tc-night," replied John Daxendale, uneasily. "Just hear them!" And, in truth, they could hear in the distance the deep baying of hounds, and the more shrill bark of a terrier. . "There's sornaone about this place .that has no right here," he added. "You're only nervous, Jack dear," she said, taking his arm, and drawing him into the room. " Come and talA to the others." The little party broke up early, for, as it happened, only two of them were staying in the house. Evelyn Kaylor was going off under the care of her aunt, to that! aunt's house,some three miles away; and, a.s the -elder lady declined to allow the horses to be kept wait- ing, there is some little hurry at their de- parture.- Miss Dorca.s Stubbs never allowed anyone to he .kept waiting if she could pos- sibly avoid it; end she boasted that, for her own part, she had never kept anyone waiting in her life. She was a large - framed, corn. fel-table -looking lady, with a shrewd, kindly face, and a somewhat direct fashion of ex- pressing herself; and she secretly worshipped her niece, and believed that no man was quite good enough for her. She hurried the lovers over their farewells now, and bundled Evelyn unceremoniously into- the carriage. "You'll have plenty of time for that sort of thing later on----,too much time, if anything, John," said the good lady. "I believe you lunch with us to-morrow. pon't be late." The earriap) rolled away, and other car- riages followed with the other guests. The firm wc.r. r Dick Munbv and Felix Goode, the lawyer. Dick was staying until the next morning, while Felix Goode was to be roused at an unearthly hour, in order to catch an early train, for a special reason of his own. The three men • watched the last carriage roll away, and then turned into the smoking-room. "I'm for bed," said Dick Munby, sleepily. I "I can always put in any amount of 23leepL-- there's something of the dormouse ab6ut me,. I think. Gocd-night—and don't talk busi- ness ! " After he had gone tl.at little dried-up man, Felix Goode, walked to .the table, And slowly mixed himself a little weak whisky and soda. In the very act of raising the glass to his lips he paused, and locLed over it keenly at the young man, who was lighting a cigar- ette; seemed to sigh for a moment, and then slowly sipped at the Qbn nt s. Anyone watch- ing the old man might have been persuaded almost that he was making up his mind to Perform a disagreeable task, and was a little uncertain as to how best to set about it. He paced about the room a little, with his shrewd face puckered into a thoughtful frown. John Baxendale, noticing him, laughed, and spoke in his cheery voice. "Why, Mr. Goode, you look as if you had something on your mind," he exclaimed. "Well, so I have," was the unexpected reply of the little lawyer. "Wien a man takes up the law, John, as a profession, he must expect to have many things on his mind—he has to become, you know, a sort, of general repository for See-ets. So it happens that I have a secret to-night on my mind— and to-night it js to become a secret no longer. In ether words, John Baxendale " Felix Goode drummed softly on the table with his finger-tips, and looked down at it— "in other words, _it is a secret you must share." "Part of ray inheritance?" asked qaxen- dale, laughingly.

"Part -of Your inheritance, my boy—and the gravest part cf ail," retorted Goode, quietly, as ha raised his •eyes for a moment to look at the young man. "To-night, when you come fully into your kingdom, and when all that NN as your father's belongs by right to you—to-night you most accept also the burden that was his, and the secret that be shared for many years only with me—and with a woman who is dead.' "A woman?" John Baxendale looked .at him curiously. "Your mother. A saint on earth, if ever there was one; and a woman deeply wronged. I have to catch a very early train, as you know, John, and I. want to get some sleep beforehand," wept on the lawyer, taking out his old-fashioned watch, and locking at it as it lay on the palm of his hand, "so I will be as brief so possible. Tell me, in the first place, my boy, what you know of yourself, and of your father and your mother. I mean, of course, your early impressions since you first knew anything at all." "My father—somewhat stern and hard with those he ,did not like—very just, but very merciless," said John Baxendale, after a moment's thought. "Fairly correct. Bat go on." "My mother— a timid, quiet woman, with a leak in her eyes .that I never quite under- stood. It was a look that might have been left as the incliblo stamp of some old trazedv—something that lißd swept over her lire, and lett her,- Changed and bro Zen- .- That's more correct still." said Mr. Felix Goode, with a sigh. "Now, what of your- self? " "Oh, there's nothing much to tell about me," replied John. "I always had rather a good time. An only son always does, you know." The lawyer slowly turned his glass round upon the table, looking down at it. He still seemed to he considering in what words he should tell .this secret that had been locked in his breast for so many years. Looking up. at last, he met the, eyes of the young man fixed questioningly upon his own. "An only son," echoed Felix Goode. "But, then, you see—you were not an only •son." In the tense silence that followed that: ex- traordinary statement the two men, the young and the eld, watching each other, could distinctly hear in the distance the bay- ing of the hounds; it seemed, too, as if a•rest- less wind had sprung up, end was moaning and murmuring about the houee. " I don't understand," said John Boren- dale at last, and his voice seemed strained and. unnatural. "I am John Bameedale., the son of John Baxend.ale—" "Dead and gone these ten years," broke in the lawyer. "But you were not an only sin. Your mother gave birth not to one child, but to two—twin sons." "Why have I never been told this? Why has it been kept from everyone?" "Well, chiefly because the story is so in- credible—so impossible to believe as havine happened in a quiet country place like this— and also because it touches an old and bitter story that everyone would have bsen glad to forget," said Felix Goode, -al'eating himoelf on a chair at the end of the table, and leaning across, the table towards Baxendale. " wrong done by your father, act to one woman alone, but to two; and a story of the bitteeest vengeance ever a human being fashioned and earned out for the punishment of another. Sit down. I'll tell yen eeverything." After a moment of hesitation john flaxen- dale sat down. .As he did so, he turned an impatient glance at the window of the room. "How thc,se dogs howl!" ho exclaimed, with something like a shudder. "When a man reaches your age, john, he doesn't need to be told that most men, and some women, have two sides to • their Eves— a face they carry to the world, nod one they carry perilous onlY to nr..p

"Never.. We searched in every direction. Advertisements were inserted in—the milers in such a fashion that they should' not attract outside attention. but should appeal to her. A reward was offered in the same way treat -should have tempted even her. But for five- and-twenty long years nothing hits happened, INA woman has never been heard of." And you lib not even }chow that my hrnther is alive?" whisuered John Baxendale. It Is utterly impoesitee to say,' repoeo Felix Goode. It is. of course, more than probable that both Johanna Cridge and the boy she stole are deed long ago. - But, cn the other hand "—the old man raised a finger im- pressively as he spoke—" it is my deity to warn you that • somewhere in the world is a man who 13 probably so like yourself that he may be mistaken for you—the actual replica of yourself in voice, and gesture, and appear- ance—and that, if that man lives, he is a hardened criminal. So much I know of the woman ; so much faith have I in what she swore she would do. You're a good fellow', John Baxendale—one of the best fellows in the world. It' the poor wretch who is your twin brether lives, he will be one of the vilest of men, with a nature twisted and tortured out of human shape." "But surely those who knew of the birth of the two boys must have said something about the matter?" euggested ,John. " How can it nossibly have becn kept aecret all them years?" "Simply because it was everyone:B bneiness to Veen it secret, for the sake of your father," replied Felix Geode. "To have told of the stealing of that second boy would have been to declare his own infamy in regard 'to the wrong he had done the woman who was the thief. The nurse who attended your mother is long einee dead. The old doctor who was present (Ved soon afterwards. In the worse of .five-and-twenty years old rumours are for- gotten, and people come to accept that which they set.e. They -,-have eeen one John Baxen- dale, son of the John Baxendaie who is dead. They have forgotten—even if they ever heard —that there was another child." " What was the boy called? " "Tie was to have been named Pith's. In her letter, Johanna Cringe supgested that he would .be brought up with that name. .Now you know- the whole story; and there is but one thing for me .to tell you, and that I lay upon you es a solemn charge, not to be for- 3often under eny eireermstanees."

"And what is that?" asked John. "That no one ever knows the truth con. cerning this het brother of voura, or the woman who stole him. Before .be came to his death - bed." the lawy,r went on, "-Your father bitterly repented the wrong he had done; but be was. neverthetesl, eager to have that wrong covered up—which is not an un• common attribute or human nature. I pro. miser] him solemnly that I would tell you the truth \Nl:en you reached your twenty-fifth birthday, and when you came into you! money ; but I also promised that it should be an injunction to yqu never to tell the story. The world believes that you are an only son —and to declare the real truth would be to bring dirace upon your. father's memory, and to rake up an old business that is best forgotten." John Barendale was silent. The whole 'thing had' been to much of a surprise that he .was at a loss to know what to do, or what tc say. Felix Goode, with another glance at his watch, was Rreparing to go to his bed, and had. moved towards the door, when Bax- endale. Put out a hand to sten him. " Suppose that it should happen that this brother of mine is- alive? Suppose that it should happen that he found out • the truthl What should I do thea ? " he asked.

"My dear boy, you have reached an age when you must judge for yourself in any crisis to which you .may come," said the old man, gently. "If it should haPpt‘n, by acme strange chance. that you come face *to face with your brother, thel it will be for you to deal with him as you thirh best ; no one else can advise you. But, in that -event, You must remember the 'man with whom you will prob- ably have to deal. , Johanna 6idge was a woman who could be merciless in any revenge upon which she had set her mind. Heaven help you if you come face to face with the man she has bent frr ,twety-five years to heT till and to 'her purpos-2 ! Now, good-night !" "You start for London early?" asked John, as •he took the old map's hand.
)?es, in a few lyydrs," replid Felix coo " Your man will call me. and 4:11,0

The lawyer ecrain, and alroc2t mechanically silmed at ids- giqFs. John Max- endale watched him, with a cniio7,ls feeling of dread beginning, as it seemed, to grip his heart. " Five-and-twenty years your mother gave birth to two boys—both equally strong and hjealthy—the one with as good a chance of life as the other. But there was someone else to be reakoned with—someone who bad every right to resent the thought that your mother had blessed your father in that way. That woman was a certain
Johanna Cridp, and elle had been a sot of companion to your mother, for .some years." " A nil my fr,f11,01•2 " John Baxendale glanced quickly at uie 0ti.21z..Q.L1at1.116-7,=i end of the tab.

Felix Goode shrui-,c,-1 his shoulders. "Your father admired .her—and. she was; I believe, pas.Tionately devoted to him. She was a strikin&y handsome woman, considerably older than your mother, but carrying; her years well. There had been scenes end troubles in the honse concerning her. She had eventually been sent away. I only knew years afterwards that after she was sent away she gave birth to a child, ‘vithin a very short time -of your own and your brother's birth, and that child died—perhars happily fo: all parties. But in her curicusly tortured, twisted nature, she nursed that wrong. Sh,a hated the thought that this wornan, who xvts in a cense her rival, could .hold ex:se children in her arms, and so triumph over her. And that was where _her curious scheme •of ven- geance came in." "That scheme of vengeance con,erred my brother, I .suppcse?" asked John Baxendalc. . „

h. Goode sn4odded hs head. " She came to the hot/se not ion after the and she pretended a deep sunnision. and a deep re- pentance concerning the scandal that had been attached to her name. For a day Or two she took up somethin7, of her old po3ition as your mother's- companion.; and then sud- d?niv cue inz;it trdine: rue of the babies with her. She left behind 3 letter, setting- forth clearly what her intention was." - '

The old lawyer get up, walked across the mom, and lcoked ova of the window into the darkness. He seemed strangely* perturbed. John Baxendale had ris2n too in his excite- ment. He waited until the old man should be more composed. _ _ _

"I cannot bear, even now, to think of what happened," said the old man at last. "I was sent for at the. time. They wanted my It seems that this woman, mad with rape anti bitterness at the (team Or ner own child, had stolen, your brother—not, as one might think, that he might take the place of the dead boy, but in order that she might be revenged alike upon your father and his wife. I remernbee almost word for word now, the *letter she left; behind; think I could almost repeat it. 'Just as 1/ou have wronged and wrecked my life, so I mean to wrong and wreck the life of this innocent boy. I take him with me into the depths into which I must inevitably sink; I drag him down with me. Mine is a curious nature. It might have been turned to beauty, and to much good. You have turned it to all that is vile. The boy shall live in the likeness of the child I have left you; but it shall be a likenesl so Pile that men shall shudder at it, and wondei how such a creature could live. There shall be two children of John. Baxendale one that lives softly, and is well fed, and well oared for, and well trained—the other a wastrel, herding with the lowest and the commonest. Yet I will be careful that the boy I take is 80 trained that he may have something of the appearance of a gentleman—something of the airs-of one. Only in all thz.t. is vile lie shall have another education, that shall leave its mark upon his soul, as you have left your mark upon mine.' " " And the child was never found—never heard of?"

too-eart is alreatv orecr:ect to take rae to ins station. Don't look so seared. Jc•hn. I'm not a bettiTag man, or I might he inclined to wager with you a pretty subf;tantivl amount that you'll never asn, yr.ur likeness in this world. Ee's piobably dead years ago. Good-nigLt !" The old man went to Lis rem, f'.l'd John Baxendale, left alone, stood for a tiine thinking over the extraordinary -story r had heard. Now he seemed to hear th,-2 cf weeping, as though that yonr:g motl: who bad been so long in 1-1.,.!r grave went at the thought cf the lost and ruined toy who had been stolen from her arms ; and would not. al together be comfoi •..?cl, crc nth th,3 one that was left. And now, stranely enough, he thought. with a .shudder. f i.,c,me strange bein like hirfself, and yet unifl...,—a weird shadow of his F.:l'A and blood and bone, with the soul of another .man. Cominp, to look at the matter more calmly, he told himself that this was but an old story, and nothing more; that if for five-and-twenty years the • man had been silent he would Le silent now. The thing Was done with—an old unhappy story, like a had dream.

He thought about it for quite a long time, and then at last decidal that he would go to bed. The room sc.:Alltd hot and oppre2sive, and ho flung open the window to get some air. And one more across the darkness he heard the distant restles !baying of .the hounds—even caught liintly the rattling of their chains as tfiey strained at them. He wondered a little why th-y should be so rest- less to-nght: "I wish I'd hail the grounds searched," he muttered.

He put out the lights in that mom, and went across the f,Yreat hall on his way up- stairs. His foot was on • the lowcst sbir when he. stopped,- listening. He had heard a faint sound.. in the big draw;ng-room towards the left. He stood perfectly still, and there floated to his ear the noise as of someone hacking or wrenching at woodwork—a grind- ing, straining sound. He shot out a hand, and turned off the electric light in the hall; and then stood still, waiting and listening again. John Baxendale was a brave man, and there was no thought in his mind of sum- moning assistance. He knew instinctively that someone was braking in', and it seemed but a natural sequel to his fears and suspicions at. the time when he had seen the .shadow move in the grounds: He softly opened the door of the drawing-room, and crept in in the dark- ness; got a momentary stirring of the heart as he felt a chill wind from outside strike in upon him, and knew- that one of the long windows had been forced open. Then, holding himself ready for an attack, he preFoed the switch of the electric light hard, and flooded the room with brilliance.

There was no one there. He looked care- fully round, and then slowly advanced to- wards th 2 •great windows, one of which was open. Between the windows hung a long mirror, and as he advanced towards it ha saw himself clearly there. He moved .nearer; and then something strange about the reflec- tion struck him—some movement of his own not responded to by the likeness in the glass. Within a foot of it almost he . put out his hand-4,nd touched not the glass, but warm flesh and blood.
In a moment he Was grappling hard with a man ho clung to him and fought fiercely. And the savage face into which he looked was his own face—as though, indeed, he had been Looking into a mirror.,

Women on Borough Cpuncils.—Aircady a number of women candidates have bi en adopted for the Borough Council elections or London next month. Although women have taken part in by-elec:ions, this will be tl.e first triennial conttst since the passing of the Act of 1967, which enables electors to return women as well as men, to serve on these Councils. Married wlmen vho pay rates are entitled to vote at these elections in London, and, if a recent decision of the revising barristter of Birmingham holds good, they are entitled to be placed on the voting lists for the Town Councils and provincial County Councils, in England and Wales, from which lists they have hitherto been excluded. In practice this reform does not amount to very mud', because there are few married womer, nut widows, v.bo pay the municipal rates. The passing of the Act of 1907 was a public recognition of the need of the the co-operation of women with men on 1( cal Govern- ment bodies, and whilst we see a lot of energy, and useless sacrifices made by the militant suffragists, it ill be interesting to note at the forthcom'ng election in Londcn, what real intertst women nrei prepated to take in local affairs.

Society Writers and their Bo' ks.—Severt.l well- known people in Society are lestowicg (fl the 'world their " Memories" or "Recollections." Lady Cardigan, who was the, wife of the hero of the Balaclava chargP, has caused something like a sterrn in the dove cots (1 society, with her " Recollections." Her reminiscences are the talk of the clubs, and quite the sensation of the Autumn season. Lady St. lieber is also shu rtly to publish her "Memor.es of Fifty Years." She is the widow of the fanacus Divorce Court—Sir Fran( is J-ulie —afterwards Lord St. Heber—who died in 1905. The writer was one of the n ost respected and gifted hc-I‘3.sses of her generation, and her book will doubt- less be accepted as a tree picture of social life in the latt3r half of the ninetee nth century. Lady Sarah Wileon's "Recollectiobs" which are to be published by Mr. Arnold in the late utumn will deal chiefly with her adventures in South Africa, before and after the outbreak of the war. Letly Sarah it will be remem- bered, was taken prisoner by the Beers early in the the war, but was exchanged for one of the captured enemy, supposed to be a horse thief. Ludy 'Butler is also to publish an account of h( r travels. She is the painter of "The Roll Call "aid lives with her husband Sir William Butler at Bansha Castle, Ccunty Tipperary in Ireland.

Cures for Rheumatism.—Many are the cures f°r rheumatism, but most sufferers find that whilst the cureg come and go, the rheumatism remoins. One of.rhet latest ideas is that celery is beneficial to those subJ2.9_ to rheumatism. It is not suggested that it is an untal's lug cure in long-standing cases. but celery contaio certa'n alkaline salts, which tend to neutralise CO ditions which give .rise to symptoms of rherreatisra'- ' Another remedy which is in use in some of the Lood°l/ hospitals, is that of bee stings. Hitherto the difilcultY has been to get the bees to stir:l; the right persoo• They are rather unmanageable things, but a coetrsvaso°, called a "bee-vaccinator" has been devised which get-: over this difficulty. " Aly Recollections " by the Countess of Cardigan and Larcastre.— In the above hook, published by Al. Eveleigli Nash, Lady Cardigan says, "I suppose I must have had some unaccountable fascination for bereaved husbands." Nearly all the men who propped to hc. were widowers. Her first hustand—iJord Cardigan—was cue, as too was the Count de Lancastre. Lady Cardigan has teen very daring in her remin- iscences, and many of her anecdotes come into touch with people still living, or with their children. Some of the tit-bits can hardly be said to be in the hest of taste, and the reflections they cast upon a number of people do not say much for the moraty, the modesty, and high respectability that is usually claimed for the social world of the late Victorian period. Lady Cardigan went out a great deal in Society, and some of her stories revive petites histoirei which those families to which they relate would prefer to forget. But if her book suggests that the latter half of the nineteenth century was no better than it should to, it is Through- out hright, clever, and witty, and oce of the most entertaining volumes of soc'al go,sips that has seen the light for many a long-day. The Aviation Costume.—The fashion journals are already c ncerning themselves as to the proper feminine c 3st ume for aviation. Soon, the enthusiasts tell us, it will be fashionable to spend week-ends in the air, and if so, it will be necessary for women to dress for the occasion. Lady Harberton will doubtless welcome that necessity, for it will hardly Le possible for a woman to goup in a 113 ing machine in a shirt. 'then perhaps in course of time we shall have the sweeping away of the Sc called "monstrous absurdities" which have character- ised womans' dress for hundreds of Tears. And. thf re is not only the inconvenience of -these absurdities. According. to Lady Harberton thelskirts is the cause of women being subject to panics in a crowd or stampede. Her dress hampers her, and the sense of danger inspires fear. Here dress reformers are on firmer ground than they are for many of their ideas, which in their revolt against conventionalism, would merely substitute one form of conventionalism for another. Warrington opened in very aggressive fashion and for a quarter of an hour the Reds were completely out- played. Warringtou's attack was often faulty, however, and the defence prevailed. EBBW VALE V. WIDNES

At Ebliw Vale, before . a large number of spectators. The homesters led at the outset, but Widnes retaliated with vigorous ploy,and McCarthy, after receiving a pass from Carr, managed to. score for the visitors, Carr successfully taking the kick. In the second bait play had not long been in pro- gress ere " Chick" Jenkins, for Eta) Vale, picked up the tall 35 yards from the opponents' goal, and splendidly dropped it over the goal posts. Two or three minutes later he made another attempt, but this time he was wide. Ebbw Vale now pressed hard, but nothing more was scored. Widnes 5 point:, Ebbw Vale 2 points.
RUNCORN STILL UNBEATEN.

About fifteen hundred spectators witnessed the Run- ccrir and Yerk match at Runcorn,the visitors bringing a fairly representAtive team. The home sid 3 were unfortu- nate in having five players absent. Richardson com- menced for Runcorn, but the visitors soon got on the attack after a forward dribble. Resuming P•isv;ood" in returning had his kick charged by Butterworth, arid the York line was in danger. Moore relieved, but Kennedy and Padbury broke away, the latter forcing his way over the line near the posts, Butterwoith failing at goal. The last-ramed player then retired injured, but just before the interval Plimmer placed a fine goal for York from almost half- way. Half-time score :—Rencorn I try (3 points), York 1 goal (2 points. Runcorn then gave a brighter exhibition, and a round of passing, in which Butterworth, Moran and Unsworth took part, ended in the last-named cross;ng the line at the corner, for Butterworth to add a goal from the touch-line. The home team pressed after this, and scrimmaging followed in the Warrington half. friampson kicked a penalty goal for Salford. Bad field- ing on the part of the home backs allowed the visitors to reach the quarter flag. Dainteth scored, the same playing goaling. Half-time n "A,' 10 points; Salford "A," two. Thd second half opened in favour of the home side, but Warrington beating off the invasion, monopolised the play. WARRINGTON ALBIONS V. CLOCK FACE. This mrtch was played at Clock Face. The matcL throughout was evenly contested and it was ratlcr hard lines on the Albicns losing through no fault of their own for the forwards and backs played P. splendid game. A word of praise is due to Meaning, the custodian for Clock Face who defended splendidly. W. Thomas for the Albions kicked off against the wind and the sun before a large crowd. During the first ten minutes Richard worked himself through to within five yards of the goal line and the referee awarded Clock Face a goal kick which was unsuccessful. Ten minutes before half-time the home team secured a goal from a corner hick, Evans, the Albii.n's goal keeper being a complete failure. Imruedia!ely afterwards the Albions pressed hard, and T. Whitfield was unfortunate en'iugh as to meet with a slight accident in the home tam's goal. -He continued to play, hut shortly after half-time mas compelled to leave the fate of the match t.-) the other placers. Half-time score :—Clock Face 2, Warrington Albions nil. Immediately on changing ends Manning, the Clock Fele custodian, saved a marvellous shot from Hunter. Manning made a splendid clearance, and the Clock Face centre -forward broke away and scored. Give and take play followed, and about Lalf-way through the second half the centre furward of Clock Face shot from about 30 yards range and the goal- keeper mis-kicked, this making Clock Face's third goal. Result :—Clock Face 3, Warrington Albions nil. TO-DAY'S MATCH.

WA RRINGTON ALBION RESERVE V. WELLEI There was a good attendance on the Liverpool-roan enclosure on Saturday to wit tins the meeting of these teams. The Albions lacked the services of several useful men but Wellfield were at full strength, the team turning out as selected. Hewitt won the toss for the Alhions and Dodds started, but Wellfield made little headway, for the home forwards got possession and rushed the ball down the field and Spooner scored with a ground shot. Hawthorne pulled Corle.ss up just outside the penalty area when the latter'player was going hard for goal. H. Cherratt altuost put through his own goal in trying to clear, the ball just grazing the cutside of' the poEt. The visiting forwards again

got possession and Corless tested Wyatt, the keeper turning the ball round the post. The .corner kick was futile. Corless heat Motley for possession and Burrows fouled Corless. All three players went down, and Motley and Corloss were injured. From the free- kick Dons scored for Wellfield. A few minutes later Wyatt saved splendidly from Col less. The Albion pressed and Newton did excellent work on the defensive, Lockhart got possession and lan down the field and scored the second goal for Welltield. Half- time : Wellfield, two; Albion Reserve. one. On resuming the Albion team was changed. Burrows restarted and the Albion made headway, but Newten cleared. Beddall made a splendid effort to reduce the lead, but his shot just missed by inches. From the goal-kick Wellfield raced down again and Dodds scored after some smart combination on the part. of their for- wards. The visitors overplayed the home team, and had it not been for Hawthorne and Wyatt the szere would have greatly increased. Taylor forced a corner off 'Hawthorne. Spooner beaded the ball away, but Lockhart returned and• Dodds trapping the ball cop- pletely beat Wyatt. Result : Welifield, four : Albion Reserve, one. HOWLEY ATHLETIC V. WARRINGTON ALI-HONS.

div.head: FOOTBALL GOSSIP.
div.p: FOOTBALL GOSSIP.
BY B. DENNIS N.
ILLUSTRATED BY JACK DODWORTH.

It is well for the football world that it has among its curiously different folk such a man aa Colin Veitch. The Newcastle ptofessional may not know it, but he has shown that he haz got more deeply into the inside of this regrettable quarrel between the Players' Union and the Football Association, and is gifted with greater diplomacy than most of those who have to do it. He may be described without undue exaggeration as the peacemaker-in-chief. It was Veitch who at the most critical period in the history of the Association game made it .possible for the; season to begin; it was Cohn Veitch who had most to do with pix.lventin.g, many of the Manchester United player.? going on strike a week ago. It is a happy circumstance for all parties alike that Veitch has been given an official status in this disput7, and if the Players be wise in the conduct of their quarrel they will not compromise themselves by a renewal of the disturbance, which with most of us had come to be regarded as practically at an end. We most em- phatically want this wrangling to cease; • even whispers of the possibility of a strike arc distaste- ful, and I enjo4n the Players' Union to proceed cautiously, and before they resort to drastic measures to consider in all its bearing what an op,h ,var would mean. 1 he F.A. and. Roberts.

And to the Football Association I would cay that they Tight very profitably pursue a policy of give and take. It was a mistake by which no good purpose can poet,ibly be served to with- hold from Roberts the " benefit " it was r,rrangc,-.1 he sliould have. It is very true that he, together - with other members of the Players' Union, is a party to a quarrel which

yet to be scttled, but a bolt having been and the offenders against the game's gov- ernment having been so far forgiven 1.1. i to be allowed to play, to receive wages for playing and permitted to craw back-pay, are circum- stances - which suggest peace; at any - rate the mapping out of a highway to an amicable understanding. I am sure that the Football Association have no desire to .do Roberfs an in justice, but I do think they might very well have grani•,:-d the request made by Roberts. Thi3 an inopportune moment for friction of any kind; the poe-sibility of a " strike " leaves a bad impression. The .)lanchestcr United players would have been very ill-advised to have refused to turn out last Saturday;- had they done so they would have Eeriously prejudiced their cause.. The obviously proper thing for the Football Association and Players to do is to came together at once and hit upon some work- ing agreement. Preston's Misfortunes.

- - .Sheffield Wecinci,:ay having waited longer for cictOrry. than for many seasons past, did not for- get to make their first. win a very substantial one. I am 'rather sorry that Preston North End sufforcd by the discovery of "form" by the Yorkshiremen. One must allays have a lindly foaling. towards Preston; they laid the founda7 ton fOf the game's wonderful popularity. Soine how. the'people at Preston have not lxen happy in the building of their team for this season. It has always struck me that if the neighbourhood of Preston were scoured many promising young- sters would be discovered. In that part of Lanca- ,hire the number of strong junior clubs is very large, and I Cannot quite unde7.stand wher9 1,11

the promising boys go to. Sur2cessors to Frank Becton and Richard Bond, to mention only two Preston youths, who made their name with North End, would be very welcome at. Deepdale. By the way, Bond is settling down fairly well at Bradfora. I have not seen the little man this season; but if he has completely recovered from his knee trouble, ho should again loom large.

The Liverpoo! Derby. When neighliours meet a Titanic struggle is assured. There is no more interesting " Derby " than that .in which Everton and Liverpool en- gage; you see all the fierceness wrought by rivalry, Nyithout any serious breaches of the rules. The latest game between tlitne clubs was a most pleasant one; it was all good sport, the were just out to play football, and they d;(1. not -allow their natural keennes to win to lead to any reprehensible happenings. Everton have a remarkable penchant for winnin7, these matches, and perhapa it is about time Liverpool were successful. There was nothing very _wrong %vial .the play of Everton; they simply could not master F.ilas Hardy, who is a sort of human octopus. Liverpool must have counted them- selves lucky when they succeeded in carrying Hardy off from Chesterfield. • He is unqueet;Cn- z!bly the greatest. goalkeeper, amateur or profes- ,ional,, Playing to-day; he will again keep"" for England this season, . surely. Everton, their downfall against Liverpool notwithstanding, are at the moment at the top of the table of merit, but it does not require deep study to see how easily they can be deposed. Sh'effield United, Breford City, Manchester United, and New- castle are well in the van. As a matter of fact, the First League_ position can be turned upside clown in a moment. The race for top pou- romPi a inona strenuous' business aT.4111
N.rth and Wcolwich, perhaps, there is precious .littie difference lyetween ar.y of the clubs.
The Arsenal's Downfall One rwast feel sorry for MacDonald, the 'Wool- wich Arsenal goallice-v, r, who had seven goals scored against hitn by the Blackburn Rovers.
He was really not .fit .to play. Ho. was a very

reat cripple-, and should -have been rested. Surely the Arsenal have a good goalkeeper in reserve. The season so Tar has gone very badly against the Plurnstead team, who, besides di,- inability, to make Feints, are not being sup- rorted by the public as they used to be. Carry- ing on a big club at Woo-lwkth is a thankless im.isiness. In these days when Chelsea, Fulham, and Tottenham are such a drawing power, are ant to fight shy of undertaking the ing and tedious journey to riumstcao umess they are sure of seeing- tip-top football. One kopes that the Arsenal officials, all of whom are v... 17 good sportsmen, will itse superior to the tioiiition which they OCCLIDV.

div.p: CROSS COUNTRY.
Opening of the Season.

The Isiverpool and District Association toad their first tun of the scason on Saturday afternoon. Starting from Rvlands'Recreation Ground, Wartingtcn twenty- seven clul.s, comprising 253 meml-ers, ran a distance of six-and-a-half rui!e4. The cluk s were made up as follows :—BirkenhealParishChurch 4, Farnworth IL 2, Liverpool H. 7, Liverpool Buttniary 1, Liverpool Gordon 1, Liverpool Gymnasium 4, Liverp,,ol Odd- fellow s 1, Liverpool Pembroke 2, North Liverpool Gymnasium 8, Prescot A.C. 5, Ravenhcad St Helens 14, Liverpool Ricbmond 5, Runcorn TatLy Ho 0, Runcorn Holy Trinity 18, St. Helens Sacred Heart 27, Sefton H. 2, St. Helena A.C. 8, St. Hel,us Rees 5, Sutton H. 24, Wallasey A.C. 1, Warrington Rylands Workmen 23, Cable Works 16, Athletio 14, United 35, West Cheshire H. 15, Wigan C. and A.C. 3, St. Austin's IL (Thatto Heath) 1. The runners, whose captain was Mr. J. T. Rimmer, after going one lap round the Recreation ground pro- ceeded acros3 Mauchester-road crcssing the canal at Paddington Locks. When near the canal the whippers- in,.G. H. llootkman and C. Howarth found themselves much in the rear and to save time did quite an unusual thing—swam across the canal. They then went over Westy Barn to Woolston and back ag .in to Man- chester-road. In the run across the country Rylands' Club showed up well. It is hoped they will have a successfnl season.

A mile from home the competitors were pulled up for the final sprint to the Recreation Ground, the seniors having a start. 'lbis race resnited in J. T. Rimmer, of Sefton, gaining piernier honours beating A. Parkinson, of Liverpe ol IL, hy tight yards, whilst C. IL Spence, of Wallasey, was placed third. S. Fran- comb (Sefton), G. W. Hunt (Warrington United), and H. J. Lyon (Ravenhead) followed in quick succesion. The time was given sA smin 28recs. The novices' race provided an exciting finish, and only four yards separated the first three home. C. Holland of the Sacred Heart, St. Helens' was placed flr.tt ; J. Price, West Cheshire IL, 2, and James Langley, Sacred Heart, St. Helens, 3. The winners of the muster pr;zes were as fellows:- 1, Warrington United, 33; 2, Sacred Heart, St. Helens, 27 ; 2. Sutton Harriers, 21. A:ter the race tea was served, and a smoking concert followed, when the prizes were distributA. The follow- ing members of the Excelsior Glee Party contributed to an excellent programme :—Messrs. J. R. DI ootfield, E. Taylor, T. Fairhurst, S. Knowles, J. johoson, A. Summer, H. Hodt,son and H. THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, ocromit 9Tv, 1[409.
The House of Commons A PREPOSTER- is to have a week's OUS THEORY. holiday. The announce-

ment was made by Mr. LLOYD GEORGE shortly after the opening of business on Wednesday, and was immedi- ately followed by many wild conjectures. It was said, for one thing, that his MAJESTY is taking matters into his own hands. There was this amount of excuse for the rumour, that the KING is undoubtedly exhibiting a close interest in the political situation. He has been seeing leading politicians of both parties and one who is of no party at all, if that is the description that is actually to be applied te LORD ROSEBERY. But we may take the liberty of saying that the KING understands the working of the Constitution far too well to act otherwise than on the advice of his Ministers. We' do not, for our own part, anticipate anything in the nature of an attempt to revive personal government. The situation is, in fact, not worth discussion from that point of view. 'There is no reason to suspect his MAJESTY'S Ministers of any deficient sense of their responsibility, or to imagine that the KING would desire to go beyond the limits observed by his prede- cessors when critical situations have pre- sented themselves in regard to the politics of the country.

The simple truth is that, though the state- meet made by Mr. LLOYD GEORGE was of an unexpected character, it was an explanation quite natural under the circumstances, and exceedingly welcome to a tired House o Commons. If there had been no adjourn- ment next week, there would have been very little work to do, and hardly any work of importance: The arrangement arrived at is one that meets everybody's con- venience. It has been called a surprising decision. It is nothing of the kind. The session has been a very long one, and it will be prolopged for a month at least after mem- bers of Parliament get back to London. The burden on Ministers has been almost too heavy to be borne. Had any medical man been called in to advise, he must have recom- mended just Such a step as that Which, in a certain probable and almost 'certain contin- gency, is to be taken. Members will have an interval of rest. They will have an oppor- tunity of studying in detail the business that will come before them .on the resumption of Parliamentary proceedings. What seems highly probable is that the time over which Parliament will be required to sit will be shortened by the adjournment. The idea that some bargain is to be made with the House of Lords we must pronounce to be simply preposterous. It is not possible to- make a bargain with the "backwoods- men," who, as it seems at present, are to determine what the conduct of the Peers will be. But even if a bargain could be made, it would involve the abandonment of a position which no Liberal Government can surrender. It cannot be said too often, and with too much emphasis, that the questions involved in a dispute with the House of Lords about the Budget are of tremendous magnitude. It is the principle of popular representation that has to be preserved. The Government, of course, cannot give way under such circum- stances, and there is no reason why it should. There is any amount of margin for conjecture as to the course which would be actually taken if the Finance Bill were to be thrown out. But there is none whatever for the belief prevalent in some quarters that the Ministry would be prepared to come to terms under conditions that Would weaken the position of the House of Commons in the Constitution.

According to Sir Gilbert ANOTHER PRELIM- Greenall's dictum our INARY CANTER. municipal elections are to be considered as pre- liminary canters for the General Election. "The Observer "reminded its readers last Saturday that " the Conservative party are in the happy position of being able to make appeal to the people with the fullest confi- dence." We should think the reminder was very necessary, for the "happy position "of the Conservative party lately has not been very apparent. For instance there was a pre- liminary canter"--with Sir Gilbert chief whip —so recently as September 13th in Howley Ward, and. at the close the Conservatives were in anything but a "happy position," unless the bottom of the poll answers to this description. Most people think that the Conservative party is on thorns, not only in Warrington, but all over the country, and if they are going to stake their reputation on a political fight locally on November Ist they may sustain another nasty fall. Out of nine retiring Councillors, no less than six are Conservative. We wonder if these gentlemen feel as full of fight as their party leaders who have nothing to lose except the afore- said" happy , position." Councillors Steel, Sankey, Ashcroft, Wilson, Vernon and Lord will be very bold " blues" indeed if they choose party politics as their battle cry in the municipal elections. In all probability when November Ist arrives the electors will hear very little about the nudget, and a good deal about bridges, rates, and sewers. The "destructive policy of the Government," as the " Observer" styles it, will be left for other critics who have no seats to lose, or we are Much mistaken'

There was much more THE TOWN talk than business at COUNCIL. Tuesday's Council meeting, and it is not too much to say that the quality of the debates has fallen to a very low standard. Several members whose knowledge of the Standing Orders entitles one to expect better behaviour seem to be qualifying as cross-talk comedians. Their proper stage is the Hippo- drome and not the Council Chamber. It is quite the usual thing nowadays for a mem- ber to be interrupted at every turn and dragged into an unseemly retaliatory kind of argument with other members. The voice and the bell of the Mayor seem powejless to maintain order, and babel, fre- quently reigns supreme. A flippant onlooker would doubtless think he had found the best entertainment in Warrington offered free, but there are some few members who honestly regret the want of decorum so evident at each monthly meeting. We do not know where the remedy is to be found. Aldermen and Councillors cannot be rapped on the knuckles when they misbehave, but it is,perhaps,not altogether hopeless to appeal to that sense of dignity which must exist somewhere in the composition of any man who values the privilege of representing his fellows on a governing body. It is a pity that the general public do not attend the meetings in larger numbers—their presence , might have salutary effect. There is no doubt that the conduct of the debates has deteriorated rapidly of late, and if some of the older members would only practice that suaviter in modo which was so often on the lips of the late Alderman Harrison they might set a valuable example which is at present sadly lacking.

The past week has been • THE METHODIST made memorable in the ASSEMBLY. annals of Methodism by the holding of the united gathering known as the "Methodist Assembly." For a number of years the uniting of the various branches of Methodism has been under discussion and three of the smaller bodies joined under the title "the United Methodist Church." It seemed impossible to effect any further organic union but on the suggestion of the Rev. J. Scott Lidgett a committee of representative men was chosen with a view to bringing together the entire forces of Methodism for the consideration of social and spiritual tasks and the discussion of the problems and pros- pects of Methodism. After two years of labour the "Methodist Assembly "consisting of 500 chosen and representative Methodists of Great Britian gathered in Wesley's Chapel, City-road, London. They were welcomed by the Lord Mayor of the city and the occasion was one of singular interest and brilliance. Not since 1796 has there been a gathering representing a united Methodism. After that year the withdrawals began, the first being in Warrington, which led to the formation of the smaller bodies. While Methodism is still far from being organically united if is something to have formed an association which includes the entire Church. Our readers may be interested to know that Mr. A. Mounfield was chosen as a member of the Committee which has so successfully brought together the varied churches, and took part in the proceedings on Wednesday last. The subject of Temperance was to the fore at that session and the large assembly was proud to learn that the Total Abstinence Movement began not in the Cock Pit at Preston but in a Methodist Chapel and under the advocacy of Methodist preachers. Readers of the " Examiner " will not need to be told that this piece of history belongs to Warrington.
Mr. Lloyd-George's MR. BALFOUR new clause giving the AS SOCIALIST. Commissioners power

to accept payment of estate duty in land, if they think fit, met with the approval of Mr. Balfour, who claimed credit• for having defended a similar proposal in 1894. At that time, Mr. Lloyd- George pointed out, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, if offered payment in land, might well ask, "What on earth am I to do with it ? " But to-day things are different. Under the Development Bill, land will be required for afforestation, experimental farms and the. like. Mr. Balfour's approval of the new clause shows how hollow is the cry that the Budget is tentative Socialism. If there were anything fearfully Socialistic in the Budget—as *there is not—this would be the most Socialistic item of all. Yet Mr. Balfour stamps it with his approval. True, tried to safeguard himself by expressing a belief that the land would not remain'in the hands of the State. But he had previously "agreed with the Chancellor of the Exchequer that this was a very convenient and cheap way of obtaining land for public purposes." If he applied the same keen dialectic to his own speeches as to those of his opponents, he would at once have seen that " public purposes" cannot be the same thing as sale to private owners.

We wonder if Crosfield's band was animated by a spirit of satire a week last Sunday night when they played "Lead, kindly light" on emerging from Parker- street to Sankey-street. The electric arc- lights had failed in this part of the town, and there was no light to lead. If things do not improve, the band might do well to serenade the Howley Electric Light Station when the head officials are on duty. **_ _ _

It was a pleasure to observe that Mr. Pierpoint was made equally welcome at both gatherings," says the " Observer " in a reference to the distribution of prizes at the Works Bowling Association meeting and at the Conservative Club. This is a very touching example of party loyalty, for we are informed that Mr. Pierpoint was in London on the evening when he was expected at the Conservative Club. It must have been the spirit and not the flesh of the late member that our contemporary saw and welcomed. * * *

The four municipal bowling greens which were sanctioned by the Council more than a year ago ara developing into a kind of hoary anecdote. When Alderman Bolton, chair- man of the Committee which deals with such things, is asked about the bowline, greens he says they are "being considered." We should not like to say that Alderman Bolton, as a brewer, has a prejudice against municipal bowling greens as being likely to take the workingman away from the public- house, but we shall certainly think if presently. * * *

The Grand Old Man of Temperance is surely Mr. Robert Cameron, M.P. Notwith- standing his eighty-four years he still repre- sents his Durham constituency in the House of Commons, and on Thursday evening last he was speaking with all the fire and enthusiasm of youth to a meeting of the Citizens' Temperance League in Warrington. The Rev. J. B. Buglass mentioned the fact that

he last heard Mr. Cameron forty-three years ago in Sunderland, and the impression he got then had not left him yet. Once heard, and Mr. Cameron is never forgotten. The wide sympathy for humanity and the deep sincerity of the man are manifest on every line of his rugged face and in every inflection of his voice. While he lives—and may it still be long—Mr. Camerson will never cease to serve, to teach, and to inspire!

" One gets really tired of railing against the Corporation for the dangerous state of the tramway track in different parts of the Borough. Public safety demands however, that the matter should not be allowed to drop. It is not the slightest exaggeration to say that Warrington Bridge, and the greater part of the roadway from there to Latchford Swing Bridge, form a positive death trap for even the wary cyclist. There are parts of the track where the setts are grooved to a depth of nearly two inches, and there are many other places where the train-rails themselves project an inch or more above the sunken road surface. Even carts and motor-cars get twisted round, and accidents are of daily occurence. - The Corporation has received complaint after complaint from sufferers, and we sincerely hope that some of the threats of actions for damages will materialise. The Committees responsible are criminally negligent in the matter, and may find themselves answerable fora fatality at any moment: The -Budget Bill has now passed through Coffirnittee, and the first stage "of the great struggle is over. Some days Will intervene before the Report stage, and the bill will be published in what may now be taken to be— allowing for certain changes on Report— almost its final shape. This will give the country an opportunity of surveying the proposals of the Government in their com- plete form. * * *

Looking back on the debates, one cannot help being struck by the extraordinary cop- trast • between the two lines of criticism brought to bear on the Government. One has been—" What tyranny I What obstinacy!" According to that theory, the Government have been deaf to reason, and have granted nothing. The other has been What changeableness What fickle- ness I" According to that theory, the Government have never known their own minds from day to day. They have always been changing. Now, one of these theories may be right; but they cannot both be right.

*-* * The result of this contradictoriness in the Opposition attitude is that the critics of the Budget seem rather divided in their claims. There are two outstanding. One is the claim to martyrdom. "See what a fight we have fought against a stubborn and unyielding Government! See how we have been treated!" The other is the claim to victory. "See how successful we have been! Look at all the concessions! They are all our prizes of war!

There, again, the opponents of the Budget must choose. For it is clear that they can- not have it both ways. The real facts of the situation lie somewhere in between these two extremes. The Government has been both firm and reasonable—firm on principles and reasonable on details. They have stood to Their guns, for instance, on the main feat Ares of land taxes; but they have granted a large number of conbessions, especially to the small men. ** * _

Now that the bill is through Committee, we can see what these concessions amount to. •!Taken altogether, they extend to the •n'ecrt"taxes the abatements already granted to ray'dg of Income-Tax. The •general prin- ciple is that there should be a level of property below which the tax does not fall: The taxes are not meant to fall on mere sub- sistence, but on large and substantial values. For that reason agriculture, being notori- ously depressed, and not having recovered from the prolonged period of difficulty, is exempted from the bill. And with it all agricultural values appertaining to unde- veloped land. .

In addition to that, all small freeholders of any kind, whether of urban or rural land, are also exempted. The limit is placed at fifty acres of rural land, and for urban properties the freehold limit is placed at £4O in London, £26 in towns of population up to 50,000, and £l6 elsewhere. Similarly, all small increments and short leaseholds are exempted, including increments up to 10 per cent. and leaseholds up to twenty-one years. Similarly, all land devoted to large public purposes is free of the taxes. That freedom will be extended to land held by charitable institu- tions or friendly societies, and to land in the actual occupation of schools and colleges.

Doctors, for instance-, are public institu- tions for the' healing of the sick and the relief of suffering. So doctors will pay only half the usual licence-duty on their motor- cars. Extending the same principle to the other taxes, there is to be no increase in death duties on small estates up to £5,000, and practically no increase of licence-duty on the small village public-house. Up to £2O annual value the increase of duty will be little more than 10s. a year. While considerate to the small man, the Budget is also very tender to the public. The public well-being is exempted at every turn. No tax falls on public parks, recreation-grounds, and playing- fields. Private grounds can also obtain exemption as a reward for giving access to the public. * * *

There is the same tenderness all through to genuine industry and real commerce. Motor-cars used for commercial purposes, for instance, are relieved of the tax on motor-spirit. There( is an extension of the relief to earned incomes, which will pay on Income-Tax only 9d. for incomes below £2,000, and is. Od. between £2,000 and £3,000. There is a special provision of exemption for land actually in the process of development, so that the Land Tax will only fall on land which is really held up from the market to the obvious detrinient • of Society. • That land certainly ought to pay, and it is the object. of the Budget that it should pay something towards the common good. A d in the £ is surely not too much. ** * _ _

Finally, the Budget is kind to children, who will be able to know, as they grow to years of knowledge, that they came as a boon and a blessing to their parents. ' For each of them carries to every " small man" a " ten-pound note" of exemption from assessment on Income-Tax.

Accident at the Skating Rink. Mr. George Darton, a young man, 0, Cawdor-street, Stockton Heath, whilst skating on the Palatine Rink last Saturday evening, sustained a fracture of the right leg just above the ankle. He was taken to the Infirmary and later he desired to be taken home and since then he has been attended by Dr. Joseph. He is progressing favourably.

HERNIA.—The new Fluid Pad Truss never gets hard and is effectual in most difficult cases. For slight cases the new Waterproof Washable Truss, which is always clean and most durable, is strongly recommended.— WHITE & WRIGHT, Surgical Instrument Makers, 93, Renshaw st., opposite top of Bold et., Liverpool.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.
Corning Events.

The Rev. E. E. Walter, of New Brighton, vill preach the autumnal anniversary sermons at Latch- bid Baptist Church to-morrow (Sunday). The penny popular concerts will be resumed in Bold-street Schoolroom this (Saturday) evening. Harvest thanksgiving services will be held at Cairo- street chapel to-morrow (Sunday), when the Rev. R. S. Redfern, of Leigh, will be the preacher. The Rev. J. S. Langley, of Kirkham, will be the preacher at the harvest thanksgiving services at Wycliffe Cockhedge Mission to-morrow (Sunday). A public meeting and united rally of Bible classes will be held in Bold-street Wesleyan Church to-morrow (Sunday) afternoon when Mr. R. Cameron, M.P., will deliver an address.

A public meeting in connection with the Warrington Women's Suffrage Society Society will be held in Cairo-street room on Monday evening. Alderman Bennett will preside and the speakers will be Miss Abadam and Mrs. Rackham The annual tea and concert in connection with the Warrington Women's Liber.:l Association will be held in Bold-street Wesleyan schoolroom on Monday, the 18th inst, Miss Truda Crosfield will give an illus- trated lecture on her travels in India. The annual sale in connection with the Brabazon Employment Society will be hell at Mrs. Frost's, Grappenhall, ou Thursday next.

" What Every Woman Knows." This successful play from the pen .of Mr. J. M. Barrie, will be produced at the Shakespeare Theatre, Liverpool next week bv the full London Company, including Miss Hilda Trevelyan. Presentation to an Ex-Constable. .

An interesting ceremony took place at the Borough Police Station yesterday afternoon when ex-P.C. John Turner, who recently • retired from the Force, was the recipient of a handsome chiming clock suitably inscribed from the membecs of the local Police Force on the completion of 25 years service. The Chief Constable made the presentation on behalf of the Force. Mr. Turner is a native of Somersetshire and joined the Warrington Police Force in July 1881. •

The Torchlight Tattoo. We would remind our readers of the grand torch- light tattoo and military display promoted by the 4th Battalion P.W.V. (South Lancashire Regiment) which will be held in Viaoria Park,. Latchford, on Thursday evening next. Eight bands, consisting -of 250 performers and including the pipers of the 10th Scottish Battalion" The-Kings" (Liverpool) Regiment will take part. There will be a night attack on a bivouac and altogether the.; proceeding should be most interesting and picturesque.

Inspector Cox. . Inspector Cox, the local inspector of the National Society of the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, will leave Warrington on Tuesday week to take charge of the society's work at Scarborough. It is five years since Inspector Cox came to Warrington from London and he has gained general esteem by the conscientious tactful and kindly way in which he has discharged his difficult duties. He will have the good wishes of his many Warring! on friends in his new and more pleasant sphere of work. Adult School. The first of a.series of fortnightly lantern lectures took place at the Adult School, Academy-street, on Thursday evening. There was a Lift attendance. Mr, J. A. Ransome presided, Mr. E. R. Braishaw (secre- tary Manchester Adult School Union) gave a lecture on "The Egypt of the Exodus." The lecturer explained, with the aid- of the lantern, the life of the Egyptians and Israelites at the time of the Exodus. He also dealt at length with the inner life of the Court and spoke Upon the architecture of that period. Mr. J. J. Firth. Police Court Missionary, Manipulated the lantern.

£65 for a Son. . Deputy Judge Sellars on Wednesday at the Altrin- cham County Court heard the application of Frank Hitchinson, of 4, Dale-street, Warrington on behalf of himself and family for compensation against Messrs. D. and S. Occleston. of Partington, for the loss of his son who was killed at their works on the 24th of April last. Mr. Noel B Goldie, instructed by Mr. Thomas S.. Steel, solicitor' Warrington, appeared for the applicant, and Mr. F. Foley, instructed by Messrs. Field and Cunninghani, solicitor, Manchester, appeared for the respondents. The respondents had paid 50 into Court but the Judge awarded the applicant £65 damages and costs on scale C.

Good Templary. The Warrington " Ideal " Lodge of the 1.0.G.T. held theis weekly meeting on Thursday evening in the Workingmen's Mission. Hall, Thewlis-street. The usual business of the meeting having been gone through, the visitors were admitted for an entertain- ment which Bro. W. Smart had arranged. Bro. Nichols presided over a very good audience. Songs were, well rendered by Bros. Shelley, Richardson, Savage, Smart, Mr. Rowlands and Sister Bernie. Recitations were given by Sister C. Jones and Bro. Sheath. Misses Smart and Bate contributed a duet, whilst Bro. Lee and Sister Lee played pianoforte solos. A. vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman for presiding and also to the artistes. An invitation was given to those who were not members to join the ranks.

Suicide of a Girl of Fifteen, A. remarkable suicide by a girl of 15 was investi- gated by Mr. Coroner Brighouse at the Police .Station last evening. The deceased was Ada Fisher, residing with her grandmotlor, Mrs. Burgess, 108 Pierpoint- street and daughter of Henry Fisher, Attercliffe, Sheffield.. The evidence disclosed that the girt had only returned on Tuesday from a visit to an aunt at Statham While there she took a bottle of carbolic acid from the mantel-piece, and an hour after returning home she was found suffering from the effects of -poison. The bottle was found in a closet at the back of the house. Emetics were applied by P.C. Holland, and the girl was hurried 'off to the Infirmary, but died soon after admission. Her relatives gave her the character of a bright girl, and no reason can be found for her taking her life. The jury returned a simple verdict of ". Suicide" and the tragedy remains unexplained. Late Councillor W. B. Roberts.

Councillor William Brittain Roberts, of Bleak House, Lymm, formerly of Wilderspool House, Warrington, until recently head brewer for Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co:, Ltd., * Wilders- pool; a member of the Education Committee and a prominent Freemason; who died on the 25th of July at Brook House, Wilderspool, left property totalling to £15;456 15s. 10d. gross and £14.745 net. By his will dated 13th May, 1908, he gives to his wife all his household furniture and effects, and his real and personal estate upon trust to pay the income to his Wife for life and then the residue upon trust to pay the income to his son Victor George Roberts, and his wife and children, failing which then to his god- daughter Irene M. K. Dowling. The widow Mrs. llilda Marian Roberts, Mr. Arthur Houle French, of The Tower, Boreham, Chelmsford, civil engineer, and Mr. Arthur James Willett, of Warrington, solicitor are the executors.

Band of Hope Merrle Meeting. On Wednesday evening the first Meeting of the above character, under the auspices of the Bold-street Wesleyan Band of Hope Society, was held in the schoolroom and was presided over by Mrs. Whitmore. During the evening a short - interesting address was given by Mr. Walter Twiss on "The importance of Band of Hope work, on the formation of friendships, and the responsibilities of sunh friendships one toward another." The following programme was given by the members and reflected the greatest credit oti each one concerned':—Pianoforte solo," The Marseillaise," Ivy Rigby ; recitation,' " Fidelity" Amy Ball ; violin solo, Harold Daintith ; solo, " Listen to the voice of Jesus," Florrie Wood (accompanied by Edith Holland) ; dialogue, " Story of two dolls,' Parthina Knight and Alice Nurse • humorous song, " I've found it," Charles Hamblett ; recitation" The Slave's Dream," Olive Player; recitation, "The Little Mischief" Gertrude Hardman ; pianoforte solo, Marie Smith ; trio " Social Glass," -Mrs. Nurse, Parthina Knight and Alice Nurse ; recitation" Down the City," Alice Nurse ; humorous song," Walking in my sleep" Charles Hamblett. During the evening light refreshments were served by a band of willing workers.
