! Personal. Much regret has been occlsioned by the resignation from the Liverpool City Council of Alderman J. W. Burgess. Mr. Burgess's native place is Frodsliam, but he spent his younger days in Warrington, where his family resided for many years. His first experience in municipal work was obtained in Warrington, on whose Town Council he occupied a seat from 1880 to 1885. His uncle had been a member of the Warring- ton Town Connell for forty years, and twice Mayor of the borough. .

-" Holy 'Trinity Parish Magazine" says :—The Vicar much regrets that owing to the holiday season a reference was omitted from last month's Parish Magazine to the loss sustained by the church through the removal from the town of Mr. Walter Shirlaw, who has acted as people's warden s'nce Easter, 1908. Mr. Shirlaw has been a member of the congregation for* some time, and previous to being elected churclite warden acted as sidesman for some years. Hi Ibusiness-like qualities made him a valuable coadjuto to Mr. Gill, and he will be much missed by a wid):, circle of friends. We wish him and his family ever prosperity and happiness in their new home i Tonbridge, Kent. Grand Scottish Concert. As will be seen from our advertising columns, a grand Scottish concert will be held in the Parr Hall on Monday, November Bth. The artistes engaged are up to the usual high standard which has characterised previous concerts held under the auspices of the Warrington Caledonian Association, and a rich treat is assured for all lovers of Scottish Minstrelsy. The proceeds will be devoted to local charities as in former years. Music Licencts.

At the Borough Police Court on Monday Mr. F. R Roberts applied on behalf of the Skating Rink Corn mittee for a temporary licence. He said the equip- ment of the building had cost £5,000. The pleasure of skating was considerably enhanced by music.—The Clerk: This is only a temporary application.—The licence was granted for 14 days.—Mr. Silcock made an application for an hour's extension of the music licence for the Palatine Rink, on the occasion of "Seaside carnival" on the 21st of this month.—Mr. Roberts, J.P. : I think it is too late myself. I strongly protest against late hours.—The application was granted, Mr. Roberts dissenting. "HERALD" KITCHEN RANGES save 50 per cent of fuel.—Agent J. S. GARLAND, Ironmonger, 51 to 55 Bridge st.,Warrington.—Advt. Buckley-street Band of Hope. The first. entertainment of the season in connection with the above was held on Monday evening in the ichoolroom when there was a large gathering of children and adults. The chair was very ably occupied by Mr. J. Richardson and Mr. T. Urmston was the speaker. There was a number of recitations including one by Mr. H. Woolley junr., a humorous— one by Mr. Woolley senr., and a Lancashire recita tion by Miss Kindon. Mr. E. Taylor contributed twa cornet solos. Other soloists were Hilda Knowles and Mr. Halliwell ; a trio by three little girls ; and a duet by the Misses Richardson. The meeting was con- cluded by singing the Doxology. B W.T.A.

The first meeting of the B W.T.A. since its amalga- mation with the Wom.n's Circle was held in the Club in Bridge-street on Tuesday. Mrs. Owen presided and an address was given by' the Rev. George Jackson, vicar of St. Linacre'to Miss Nellie Jones sang two solos. Tea was served by the invitation of Mrs. Own On her retirement from the presidency. Miss Duttcn proposed and Mrs., Gunnell seconded the vote of thanks. Later a committee meeting was held and ti e • following appointments were made for the ensuing year.—President, Mrs. Simpson, vice-presidents, Mrs. Owen, Mrs. Garnett, and Miss Dutton; treasurer, Mrs. Harvey Cook ; secretary, Mrs. Letheren. Mrs. Simpson added a few words after her appointment as president. Warrington Women's Circle. - -

_ Mrs. Smethurst presided at the Circle on Sunday, and a practical address was given by Mrs. Dodds. Miss Maud Hipkiss, who is always weleome at tl e Circle, sang "Angels ever bright and fair "and "Sun of my Soul." The Mayoress, Mrs. Forshaw, presented 63 books gained by attendance during the first session,. On Monday evening Miss Parker and Miss Bell started the musical drill. On Wednesday evening an interest- ing lime-light lecture was given by Mr. O'Callaghan, organising secretary of the Anti-Vivisection Society, Dr. Joseph took the chair and made a speech on the subject. Next Monday evening Mr. Robert Cameron, • M.P., is expected to speak and Mrs. Cameron will sing. Rise in the Price of Leather. The tanners of this district held an important meet- ing at the Patten Arms on Tuesday, and decided to raise the price Of leather immediately a penny in all classes. We underftand that the tanners in other parts of the country are following this lead. War- rington and District is the largest centre of the pro- duction of sole leather in this country, and there is little doubt that they will be able to establish the advance. Hides have proportionately risen considerably more than leather, and, the tanners claim that on present prices they are losing money on every hide put in, and that if they do not get an advance they will cease putting in. The following were the resolutions passed "That we, the tanners of Warrington, Liverpool and Districts realizing it is impossible to avoid a serious loss by selling leather at present prices recommend all tanners to sell no more leather except at prices at which it can be replaced by hides at current values, and consider that a further immediate advance of at least a penny per p)und should be made in all classss." "That we ask the Committee of the United Tanners' Federation to convene a meeting of the tanners of the United Kingdom in London on Tuesday afternoon November 2nd to consider the then existing positions and the advisability for a further advance in the price of leather."

PEVERIL " FIRE GRATES Still unsurpassed, Inspection invited.—J. S. GARLAND, Kitchen Range and Stove Warehouse, 51 to 55, Bridge at., Warring. tom—Advt. Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay. The Women's Bible Class connected with this Mission had the annual tea meeting on Tuesday evening, about 120 sitting down to tea in the school- roam. The after-meeting was presided over by Mrs. Crosfield (of Colwyn Bay) the president of the class. Miss Morland (of New Zealand) who accompanied Mrs. Crosfield ois the platform, gave an extremely interest- ing and able address relative to her travels. Mrs. Forster and Mrs. Highley rendered songs. and Mrs. Davies and Mrs. Swarbrick a duet. Mr. F. Atkinson was the accompanist. Recitations were given by Mrs. Tate and Mrs. Barlow. During the evening the secretary of the class (Mrs, Brimelow) read the annual report, which showed a slight reduction in membership since last year, but that a good work had been done. The visitors had worked with unt'ring zeal, paying over 250 visits during the year to the sick members and friends in the district. The accounts showed an income during the year of £24 19s. 2d. (raised by collections in the class and by eoncerts and socials), and the expenditnre £lB 15s. 11d., leaving a balance in hand of £5 3s. 3d. —Mrs. Crosfield, in commenting on the report, expressed her pleasure at being present, and hoped that the coming year would be a very successful one with the class.—Mrs: Moore, the leader of the class, voiced the thanks of the members to Mrs. Crosfield, Miss Morland, and all those who had attributed tcr make the gathering a success. TABLE AND HANGING LAMPS, new designs DOW showing.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt. " Wit and Humour." At a meeting of the Warrington Certificated Class Teachers' Association, held in the Wycliffe Memorial Hall on Saturday morning, under the presidency of Mr. I. Bowen, Mr. J. Armstrong read a paper or "Wit and Humour," in which he traced the 'develop- ment of wit from the 'old meaning of IN isdom on knowledge, as in the word Witenagemok-, through the writings of Lyly, Ben Jonson, Crashan-, Dryden, Pope, &c., giving examples from each illustrative of the changes which have taken place in the _popular con- ception of the meaning of the term. Humour was treated similarly, to show its development from the once accepted theory of . physiology, that individual character and disposition depended upon the existence of " humours " or fluids in the human body. Extracts from Ben Jonsca and Shakespeare were given to show how universally this heory was accepted. Numerous examples, anecdotes , were supplied to show the close unibn which exists between the intellectuality of" Wit " and the emotionalism of "Humour." The national character- istics in Wit and Humour were next dealt with, America, Scotland, and Ireland each contributing illustrative examples, while the slow and ponderous wit of the peasant was compared with the nimble and keen wit of the city streetNarab. (Applause).—On the proposition of Mr. F. Longsbaw, seconded by Mr. Malcolm, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Armstrong.—The secretary (Mr. G. Newburn) reported that the Annual Conference of the National Federa- tion of Assistant Teachers had been held at North- ampton on the 24th and 25th September, and was a , striking success.

But when the kidneys are weak and inflamed they cannot.keep up with their great work, and so the poisonous waste is lelt in the blood, and the whole body is being slowl) poisoned.

div.head: RUNCORN CASE.
div.p: RUNCORN CASE.

Willism Kirkham, a labour employed at Messrs. ' Crosfield's, and living at 5, Gandy's lane, was charged at the Police Court on Monday, with stealing from the works of Messrs. Crosfield and Sons, Ltd., a quantity f soap and emery cloth and paper, valued at 135., the property of the Company.—The Chief Constable said that about six o'clock on Saturday evening Detective Reddingtan, Inspector Williamson and other officers were on duty in Gands's-yard Mating inquiries into another wetter, when Reddington saw a woman go to No. 1, Candy's-yard with something bulky in her apron. Reddington went to her and asked aka she, had got there. The woman replied "That's no business of yours," and went away. The officers followed her to the house, which turned ,out to be the prisoner's. On searching her Reddington found 12 cakes of soap in her apron. They aroused the prisoner, who was in bed asleep at the titre and asked him to account for his wife's possession of the soap. He then admitted having stolen it from Crosfield's, and also showed them 68 tablets of soap in a tin box. He was brought to the Police Station and on being chareed said "I have done it."—Mr. ,F. R. Roberts, solicitor, appeared on behalf of Messrs. Crosfield, and said he had been in:tracted to press that case very strongly as they had had infinite trouble with thefts of that kind. They hed found soap stored in secret places in order that it, could he removed without trouble. They had also discovered men with secret pockets, which enabled them to take soap out of the premises. That, however, was not the most serious aspect of the case. Through those thefts all the men, women, and young people working there were thrown tinder a cloud of suspicion and if anything of that kind occurred again it might be necessary for every one leaving their employment to be searched. The firm felt very strongly that they would not have to do that as the great majority were honest and it was their desire to do that which was strictly right in their employment. He hoped that the bench would make an example of the case. His clients were very sorry they had to do so but they were -unable to deal leniently with the matter, on the contrary they asked the bench to deal very severly with •prisoney—The Chief Constable said prisoner gave them no trouble with regard to the theft and did not deny stealing the soap. He said the property was Messrs. Crosfleld'st whereas they might have had a great deal of trouble in proving the owners. Prisoner was serving on the Army Reserve and in two years would complete his time and if he was convicted of that theft he would be discharged from the service. He (the Chief Constable), however appre- ciated all that Mr. Roberts bad said.-111r. Roberts said his clients wish was that siva would not alter the magistrates judgment in any way.—With reference to the Chief Constable's statements as to prisoner giving the police all the help possible. Anyone would know that the man did not come by all that soap honestly. He again asked the magistrates to give prisoner severe punishment so as to make an example of him for intencl:ng wrong doers.—Alderman Evans: What was the occupation of this !nee in the works ?—Mr. Roberts : A labourer.—The Clerk (to prisoner) : Have von any family ?—Prisoner: Yes, two.—Alderman *Evans : How long have you been employed at the works ?—Prisoner : Five sears last February.—The Bench then retired to discuss the matter privately, and on their return the Mayor said they bad taken a lenient view of the case as it was prisoner's first appearance-, and he would be fined 40s. or one months' imprisonment with hard labour.—Mr. Roberts said he had to congratu- late the police on such a 9mart capture which was very creditable to them. BOOKMAKERS CAUGHT. HEAVY PENALTIES.

At the Borough Police Court on Wednesday,two young mtn, Walter Page, a greengrocer, of 43, Pt iestley-ttreet and Richard Bradford, iron worker, 6, Wakefield-street were charged with loitering in a passage at Quay-fold, Bank Quay,for the porpoie of betting the previous day.— Detective Reddington said that at a qutrter to two the previous day he proceeded to Quay-fold, and in conse- quence of what ha was told be went to the passage there and saw the two prisoners. A number of workmen went away. Witness stw Page with a book in his hand making entries in it and Bradford was looking over his shoulder as if dictating to Page what he should put in. A woman ran to the prisoners to tell them that witness had seen them, but it was too late. Page said "It is all right. We are caught." On the way to the Police Station, Page said "Let him (Bradford) go, I will stand for all. At the Police Station witness found 91 betting s!ips on the man Page, 4S in his pocket and 46 tied up in a lag. In Bradforct's possession he found six betting slips and also a book containing the number and names, with the cash opposite them. On comparing the names on the slips with the n.trnes in the book, he found they corres- ponded. Witness charged both with the offence, and Page replied "I am guilty" and Bradford "It is just my luck."—Bradford asked that the case might be adj3urned for a few days in order that he might get legal aid.—The Bench refused the application on the ground that he had had sufficient time to consult a

solicitor.—Bradford (to Reddington) : You said you saw me looking over Page's shoulder.—Reddington : Yes.—Bradford : You are wrong, I did not speak a word to him.—Chief Inspector 'Williamson said he had examined the boas and slips very carefully and both corresponded.—Page said be wanted to speak a word on behalf of Bradford. The latter went up to him on the day in question, and he did not know what he went for. Bradford bad not assisted him in any shape or form in street betticg.—At ter mach private coLsultation the bench imposed a fine of £lO and costs each or two months imprisonment.

Warrington Borough Court. SATURDAY.—Before Messrs. J. H. Hayward (chairman), A. J. Jolley, J. Upson, and T. Pemberton. OBSCENE LANGUAGE AND TEIREATS.—John Johnson, Barbauld-street, was charged with using obscene langulge in Orfo:d-lane, the previous day and also with uslng threats towards Edward Plinston, whereby he was afraid prisoner would do him some bodily injury. Edward Plioston, residing in Orford-lane, said he went into his shop about 5 o'c'ock and there found the pr:saner, who was swearing at his wife. Witness said "Better language here; please just clear out." Prisoner refused to go and so witness put him outside where- upon he challenged witness to fight and said what he would do for him.—P.C. Green spoke to arresting prisoner.—The Chief Constable said prisoner was a saw sharpener, and on being refused a saw to sharpen he used mast fifthly language.—A tine of 10s. and costs or 14 days was imposed.

"K REGVLA MELEE."—John Joseph Cbrischolli, Ship-yard and Angelo Chrischolli, Ship-yard, were each fined ss. and costs each for wilfully breaking nine panes of glass at the dwelling-hoose of Peter Kenny and also with assaulting Sarah Kenny at the same place and time.—The Chief Constable: said that there was a regul.,r melee in Ship-yard that night and sommonses would ensue.
MOND AY.—Before the Mayor (chairman) Alderman Smethurst and James Evans, Councillor Wilkinson And Messrs. S. Wright, W. Robe, T. Locker, and G Pilling. _ _

Two MONTHS FOR BEGGING.—John Baker, Bank- street was sentenced to two months imprisonment for begging in Bold-street the previous day. The Chief Constable said the man did nothing else but beg. SENT TO A HOME —Elizabeth Holbrook, of Watkin- street, was charged with being an habitual drunkard as defined by the Habitual Drunkards' Act.—The Chief Constable said that the woman was before the court seven days ago and the case was adjourned in order that arrangements might be made to get her into an Inebriat s' Home. He had been in communication with the Lange Home near Preston, and hadafgot a reply saying that they were willing to receive the woman.—Alderman Smethurst sad that be would like to give her one word of comfort before she went. He had visited the home and she would be quite satisfied on getting there. It was like a huge mansion with splended gardens, walls and fields and everything thit they des:red. The only thing was that she would be kept there until her time had expired.—The Chair- man : It is out of pure kindness that we are sending you there.—Alderman Smethurst: Yes.—The Chair- man : I think a lot of people would like to go there.— Alderman Smethurst: It is a lovely ptace.—Th9, woman was sent to the home for three years.

TUESDAY.—Beforti 11ressrs. IL Roberts (chairman) J. Rymer Young, and C. Jackson Holines. STABBED WITH A KNlFE.—Edward Sauce, of Glass House Raw, was charged with committing an aggra- vated avault upon Martha Green and also with using threats towards her.—The Chief Constable stated that on the 22nd of September, the complainant was at a house in Cross-street in oomrany with her dsughter and mother woman. They had been drinking beer together. She left the house at a quarter to six. As she was going it was alleged, prisoner struck the woman with some weapon, on the head which caused a serious injury. She collapsed and knew nothing more. She was taken to the Infi,mary and no less than eight stitches were placed in the wound. Prisoner was a thorough blaggard and was continually assaulting her, and he (the Chief Constable) asked the bench to inflict the heftiest peralty possible.—Ma aka Green c3rroborated the Chief Constable's statements.—Elizabeth Faulkner said she hcard prisoner say after he bad assaulted the WOMAP, thit be would go back and finish her. He also threatened Mrs. Green's daughter.—Prisoner was se2tenced to four months' imprisonment for the ntsault, and for the thrcats was bound over to keep the peace for twelve months in two sureties of £5, or in default another three months' imprisonment.

ASSAULT ON Tiff: POLlCE.—Thomas Lynch, a lance - corporal of the 4th Bat talion,Kings' Liverpool Regiment was charged with having been drunk and disorderly at Friar's Gate the previous nightand also with assaulting Police Sergeant llesp while in the execution of his duty.—Sergeant Hesp stated that at 10 30 the previous night he wis on special duty at the Palace and Hippo- drome when he was called to prisoner who bad been ejected for making use of obscene language. Prisoner was drunk and refused to go away on being requested. ' On witness approaching him, prisoner took to his heels and ran for about og yards and then fell down end with the assistance of Sergeant Cooper they managed with great difficulty to get him to the Police Station. On the way prisv'ner deliberately kicked witness on the legs.—Tho Chief Constable said that presumably prisoner had a good character or he would not be carrying his stripes.—A fine of 10s. and costs or 14 days was imposed. WEDNESDAY.—Beforo Mr. C. White (chairman), Alder- man Smethurst and Dr. Joseph. 'DRUNK AT 79.—Elizabeth Bennett, an -old and feeble woman last from Widnes, was chargEd with being drunk in Ilorsentarket-street the previous day.—She stated

that if she lived until November she would be SO years of age —She was ordered to go to the Workhouse. FRlDAY.—Before the Mayor (chairman) Alderman Smethurst Messrs. H. Thornton, T. Locker and G. Piling. ALLEGED THEFT OF BRASSE3.—Edward Duffy Kendrick a man of tramp !Me appearance who was charged at the Borough Police Court, last Friday with stealing two dozen knobs, eleven lochs, and tools the property of some person unknown, was again brought up.—The Chief Constable stated they had aszertainal that he was aconvict en licence. As they had been unable to find the owners of the articles so he asked for a flat t'ner remand of a week.—The remand was granted. BEGGING AND ASSA CLT.—Tbomas King, of no settled abode, was charged with begging in Winwick- road.—Detective Reddington s' ated that on taking pr7soner into custody for teg ging he threw himself on i the ground taking witness with him, and butted him about the head and face. He then ttfruNl a ' somersault and tried to kick witness. Witness had the end of his finger takea oft with a kick from the prisoner. Witness then called upon a young man named John Kennedy who assisted him. After go•ry, for a short distance prisoner tried to trip them both up. On getting into Winwick-street they got the assistance of P.C. Wood and managed to get pi isoner to the Police Station. ,Witness had a rough time of it before he got the assis,tance of Kennedy. —John Kennedy gave evidence and said that in his opinion the man was a violent nistomer. The Chief Constable said prisoner. had a very tad character, he admitted serving three years' penal servitude and had to serve the full period as he had boct all his marks while there. He was evidently a thorough rascal. Prisoner was sentenced to three months' imprisonment. Kennedy was thanked for his services rendered to the police.

div.head: Bewsey-road Wesley Guild.
div.p: Bewsey-road Wesley Guild.

Members and friends of the Bewsey-roa:1 Wesley Guild to the number of about 80 enjoyed a social evening on Monday in the Lecture Hall, adjoining the Church. Various games of a nature compastible with the occasion were indulged in and the event was a great success. During the evening Mr. J. E. Hannan gave a solo, and Mr. Charles Sinclair sang "A Sore." Mr. Barlow rendered a humorous recitations. The programme. for the season is aa excellent one and includes what are sure to be popular—two debates entitled "Should the nation be in arms" (November 291 h) and" Is the Con- quest of the air an advantage?" (February 2lst.)

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

Mr. R. Mile presided over the meeting of the society on Sonday last. Mr. R. J. Peake gave an address upon "The Power of Sin." He dealt at length with the great foe of man. He said that man could he a great sinner, and yet those around him be unaware of that f.17-‘t. The heart of man was deceitful, whether manl- tested or cloaked. The man to be honoured was he,who was continu illy fighting agrin t sin in e •ery form, either in hinurelf or in others, and nothing but the help of G•rd, would enable him to conquer. Miss L. Duck- worth sanz "Thy King "which was well rendered. Mr. W. H. Payion, Mlle. Ilic: presided at the organ. Mr. C. Cotton also took part in the meeting. The secretary welcomitd one nem member. The meeting -closed with sing:ng " 0 happy day that fixed ray ch3ice."

div.head: Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church.
div.p: Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church.

The Rev. Dingley P. Fuge preached in the Bowser!. road Wesleyan Church on Sunday even'ng. He triiik his text from 13 Genesis 11-12. He said that few ideas had fascinated man so much as the power of choice which God had given him. He gave t him the greatest of all His earthly gif;s—free-will, knowledge of right and wrong and the ability to choose. The preacher described the incident of how Lot chose to leave Abraham, to feed his fl,ck on the pla;as of Jordan and lire akng with his wife and daughters in Sodom. Lot at the time th ,u.;ht it was a good choice for his riches would enormously increase, but as it turned out it was ,•otherwise. Wsen Gid destroyed Solom, his wife, daughters and herds perished, cud then Lot. knew that he bad chosen wrongly. Continuing, he askel how we judged a men. Did we not judge a !ran by the size of his home, or whether he paid his rent quarterly or weekly? Did we not judge him by the number of4his servants and the horse power of his motor car? He said that when Lot went to feed his flocks on Jordan he had to go and live in Sodom. He compared that to when a man *Rh a small income sent his daughter as a 1 ar ; aid into a public house. Tee man slid there was no harm, but then there was a risk. She went in the direction of Sodom Wealth had nothing to do with happiness. He did not hold any brief for poverty, but when a man had all the necessaries of this life and wholesome work he bai all the essentials of happiness. W.-all h could do many things. It could pr;)vide a man with a wondrous sourc3 of well doing. It was not money that was guilty, it was what men did with it. Wealth and happiness had nothing to do with one, another. The things that made for happine; were these :-1, that a man's heart be right with his Maker— and until a man was right with God there was no room for happiness; 2, that what a man was, mattered more than what a man had; 3, that the next world was more important than this. Cmcluding, he said that if tb4s life were important—which it was—how much more important was the life beyond.

div.head: HARVESF FESTIVALS.
div.p: HARVESF FESTIVALS.
BRICK,STR,EET INDEPENDENT METHODIST
CHURCH.

Tho harvest festival serv:ces were held on Sunday and Mobday. Ta o sermons were preached on Sunday by Mr. William Mort of Lyrom. At the moiaiug service he delivered a very helpful sermon to a fairly good congregation from the words," Thou visitest the earth and a aterest it,' Psalm lxv. 9. In the afternoon Miss H. Howell sang "The Better Land " with good eft-et. Mr. William Wright gave an address to the scholars and teachers. At the evening service Mr. Mort. preached an eloquent sermon to a crowded congregation from the text I w:I1 speak of the glorious honour of Thy Nl,jesty, and of Thy wondrous works," Psalm cxlv. 5. The anthem "Sing to the Lord of the harvest" was sung by the choir in a very creditable manner, the solo part being taken by Mr. William Barton, jun. On Monday evening the usual entertainment and fruit t auquet was held, the chair being taken by Mr. James haw. Songs were given by Miss Foclen and Miss Bincroft and Messrs. B. Hodgson and %V. Barton. The humorous items were supplied by Mr. S. Aukland.
PRIMITIVE METHODIS r CHURCH, KNUTSFORD-ItOAD.

The harvest thanksgiving services in connection with linutsford-r.ad Primitive Methodist Ctratch were held on Sunday last, when two sermons were preached by Mr. Joseph Spruce, of Preston Brook. Adverse weather interfered with the attendance at the morning and after- noon services but in the evening the church was crowded A musical service was given in the afternoon by Legh-street choir when the following items were rendered in a satisfactory mariner : —.A otheras, "Oh taste and see " (Goss) ; " They that sow in tears" (Batson) ; " Lead kindly light" (Buck) and "Abide with me "(Dunstan) ; solo, "What shall the harvest be ?" Miss R. Brown ; solo, "The Gift," MiEl E. Hewitt; solo, "My hope is in the everlasting." Mr. S. J. Hamilton ; solo, " Wheat end three." Miss B. Brown. The Rev. J. B. Bugloss prclide? Misses E. Spruce and A. Titchett were the accompanists. The church had been very tastefully decorated by the ladies of the congregatioo. At the evening sot vice the Excelsior Glee Party rendered Lead kindly Light,' and" Remember Me," Mr. J. Monks conducting. On Monday evening a ft lit banquet was held, presided over by Mr. G. Faulkner, of Penketh. The Co-operative Male Voice Choir conducted by Mr. 3. Monks rendered

the follow, ing pieces :—" Soldiers Chorus" (Gornod), "In Absence " (Buck), and "The Crusaders," the solo in the latter being effectively taken by Mr. Fairhurst. The solos "Down in the dr )1.3 " and "Sancta Maria" were well interpreted by Mr. I'. Atwell. A sale of fruit, vegetables, &e., concluded the proceedings. WARRINGTON RAGGED SCHOOL.

The harvest festival in connection with the [tagged School Mission was held on Sunday. The mission hall was tastefully decorated by the teachers and workers. There .ras rather a poor attendance in the afternoon, owing to the unfavourable weather. The service corn - emenced by singing" Grr Lt God as seasons disappear" followed with prayer by Mrs. Simpson. Mr. Henry Wright read the lesson. Mrs. Simpson gave a very interesting address taken from St. John iv. 35 "He that reapeth receiveth wages." After the following hymn had been sung, "Sing to the Lord of Harvest," Mrs. Simpson concluded with prayer. At the evening service there was a marked improvement in the attend- ance, the hall being full. The service opened by the singing of" Lord of the Harvest once again." A solo entitled "Wheat and Tares " was rendered by Mr. Walter Wright in a praiseworthy n.anner. Mrs. Moores addressed the congregation -from the words "I have finished the work which Thou gayest me to do." lee children sang the hymn "They that waitupon the Lord." Mrs. Marsh concluded with prayer. The music at each service was supplied by members of St. Barnabas' Orchestral Society. The organist was Mr. J. Blakernore and the conductor Mr. F. 3. Owen. On Monday even- ing a concert and fruit Lanquet were held. Alr. James Dodds presided over a good attendance. Selections were given by members of St'. Barnabas' Orchestral Society. Miss Oakly and Mr. Iddon gave a piano; forte duet and Mr. Dennett and Miss Baines rendered solcs in a very effective manner. Mr. Watts contributed two violin solos. Mr. Dodds gave the children some very good advice, eLpecially the boys with regard-to being diligent at school. He stated that they had better opportunities for acquiring knowledge than he had when he was a boy and that there was no position in the country too high for them to aspire to if they would be studious and grow up to be sober citizens.
As Mr. Dodds left the platform the children care three hearty cheers. • The concert was brought to a close by the singing of the ntional Anthem.
SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN CHURCH.

The harvest festival services in connection with Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Church, were held an Sunday last. The Rev. F. W, -Kern ick preached both morning and evening. In the evening he took his text from Haggai i. 6, and in the eVening be preached ftom Matthew v. 45," Thit, ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven ; for He meth His son to riee on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust." During the evening service the choir gave a splendid rendering of the anthem "Praise Him : " There was a fruit banquet on the Mandy evening and eongs and lecltatlon3 were given by several members.

div.head: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
VISIT OF LORD WOLMER. ----- Churn and State.

Special interest was taken in the meeting of the Warrington ParliAmentary Debating Society on Tues.:- thy evening, when Viscount Wolmer gave an address on the famous Oaford Union Debating Society. There was a large attendance of members of the House and a!so of the general public. The SPEAKER (Mr. Chatles Plinston), said the Oxford Union Debating Society bad produced some of the best speakers in England on both the Conservative and Liberal sides of the House of Commons. He wished to say that Lord ‘Volmer was there as the guest of the society and not of any particular party. They hoped that whatever party toot; their place as the Govern- ment of the Society they would be able to secure some eminent gentleman on the opening night of the session. (Applause). Lord Womug gave a delight-fat retrospect, with many humorous touches, and the references to ti,e eminent politicians who have been connected with the Oxford Union Society were much appreciated. He pointed out that the S:iciety, which came into existence early in the nineteenth century, to discuss sbcial problems, was at first discourage by the authorities of the University, and on one occasion the proctors of the University, who played the part of a sort of academic policeman, interfered at its meetings and forbade the discussion proceeding any further. It chanced that the President of the Society was Mr. Wilson-Patten— (applause)—afterwards Lord Winmarleigh, who rose and said to the procters who interfered, "Sir, this house has received the proctors' message. It will send the answer to the summons by an officer of its own." (Applause.) That speech was made in a spirit worthy of the Speaker of the House of Coalitions or the Speaker of the Warrington Debating S roiety. (Laughter.) The authorities of the UniverAty were so impressed with the dignity of the behaviour of the Speaker of the Oxford Union Society that from • tint moment they desisted from their attempts to discourage Ds discussiors. Lord Wollner referred to the opening of the pre-rent deb,ting hall in 1573 by the then Chancellor of the Exchequer, Sir Stafford Northcote, and mentioned that in addition to the !arc() ball, the society possessed a library containing 40,000 volumea,ancl a aarden of about an acre in area, which was used by the members in the summer. The Society was entirely managed by young gentlemen between the ages of IS. and 20 and it ba-1 now got connecting I:nks with similar bodies through- out England and even on the Continent. Perhaps the most fa-mors member of the Oxford Union Society who ever existed was

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE

(applause)—who throughout his active membership was the strongest of strong Tories. (Loud laughter). He was secretary of the society for some time, and the society now peeseesed priceless records of minutes written in Mr. Waistone s own handwritine. He had looked at many of them li'mself, and they Were most interest lug to read. _ There was one record which would be interesting to members of that society. it was on November 11th, 1830, when a motion was proposed con- demning the action of the Duke of Wellington's Government, which was going to admit the terrible principle of Catholic emancipetion, and the thought of this aroused the Tory Mr. Gladstone—(laughter)—to the height of righteous angbr. The motion was eventu- ally carried by a majority of one, and that vote, of course, was given by Mr. Gladstone himself. It was written in the minutes under the record Of the result " Tremendous cheering from the majority of one." (Laughter). What the scene was he could not qu'te imagine. He did not know whether Mr. Gladston rose in his seat and cheered tremendously or what happened —(laughter)—but the next week it was discover .d that some memberhad scratched this out and now it c only be real in the minute book by holding it up to the light. The page was nearly scratched through with a penknife, and at the next meeting of the society Mr. Gladstone drew attention to the practice of hon, mem- bers of defacing the minutes of the society. ( He would give another interesting story of Mr. Glad- stone. Mr. Gladstone owed his entrance ,into political life eatirely to the Oxford Union Society. He made a speech. a very Tory speech. He (Lord Wolener) forgot the particular oecasien ; but its eloquence was such that the Duke of .Newcastle, who happened to be listen- ing in the gallery to the debate, immediately offered Mr. Gladstens the mmbership of a rotten borough at his (the Duke's) disposal, and Mr. Glabstone entered the House of Commons as the result of this,speech. Oh! these dukes how they harass us! (Laughter) It was an interesting fact that the old system of rotten boroughs gave a young man a very much better chanco than many had now. For instance, Fox was pat into Parliament for a rotten borough at the age of 19, and the younger Pitt was made a memher of Prelim-ilea by the same process at the age of 21, and Canning, the son of a minor actress, was pit into Parliament at the age of 21 simply because some local grandee had heard that be was a very good speaker. It was interesting to note that Mr. Gladstone Was the last of that class to be put into the House of Commons, being a great man earlier than he otherwise would have been. The only other matter of interest in the earlier years of the society centred in the member- ship of Mr. Gladstone 's rival, Lord Salisbury— (epplause)—who was 18 years younger. than Mr. Gladstone; he saes then Lord Robert Cecil, a strong Tory. He never rose to the position of president of the society, but he was secretary and treasurer. • On the rolls of the society were miny famous men, including the Marquis of Dufferin, Lord Coleridge, Lord Randolph Churchill, Lord Goschen, I..nrd St. Aldwyn, Sir William Phillimore, Lord Morley, Mr. Ibyce r. Asquith, Lord Curzon, Lord Milner, Lord hfiddel Mten, Lord Hugh Cecil, Lord Percy, Mr. Hillaire Mr. j. A. Simon, one of the corning men of the Liberal Patty, and one of the most recent of the brilliant speakers of the society war, of course, Mr. F. E. Smith, K.C.. M.P. (Applause). Waen the society celebrated its jubilee it showed the prominent position it had arrived at in the eyes of politicians by the large number of eminent men who had once been .its members and who were present at the dinner. It would celebrate its centenary fifteen' years hence, and it would be able to muster a goodly fellowship of politicians on that occ-ssion. (applause). It was interesting to look back on the opinions of , some of the members of the society. They were not ,1 the Fame as those tkey held afterward. He Lad alluded to Me. Gladstone. Mr. Asquith was always known a.s a brilliant young Liberal, and as president of the society he was succeeded in after years. by three of his sons, which was a record. There was one young Liberal whe succeeded Mr. Asquith in the president's chair very closely, whose name was Alfred Milner. It was noted that the present Lord Robert Cecil when at Oxford was a staunch Protectionist. (Laughter). On one or :asion when the members of the Cambridge Union visited Oxford, Mr. Austen Chamberlain, who was then president of the Cambridge Union, made a speech which was strongly in favour of Free 'rrads (Laughter). It was very odd that the Cambridge Union Society had not produced anything like as many grett men as the Oxford Union Society and that whereas both Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman and Mr. Balfour were undergraduates at Cambridge neither of them belonged to the Cambridge Union Society. When on one occasion he (Lord Wolmer) went as a member repressnting the Orford Union Society to attend a debate at Cambridge he remembered noticing that the only picture of any note that hung on the wall was one of the late Sir William Harcourt—(applause)—whereas the Oxford Union bad a full 100 or 150 pictures. It showed the difference between the two Universities— that while Oxford was more dialectical and interested itself in political and theoretical subjects, Cambridge devoted Itself more to mathematics and natural science. Lord Hush Cecil once told him that he thought the Oxford Union Society was the most difficult audience he had ever spoken to in his life. He thought that as an undergradtt tte, and when he returned as a guest of honour he Experienced the same difficulty. Mt Masterman, be believed, bad said the same thins. The reason, he supposed, was because the Oxford Union vss formed of so many different sots of s-eople. There was no one -line that wonld appeal to one's whole audience the whole time. Visitois to the Society were often surprised to see on the benches twenty or thirty., black members. -That simply showed how very wide was the membership of the Oxford University. (Applause). They welcomed mem- bers from India and Africa who added very much to their enlightment on subjects of which they could speak with first baud authority. In the same way they enjoyed the advantage of having Rhodes scholars,— Colonials, Americans and Germans, from all parts of the world. They were also complimented by visits from Labour members from Ruskin College who spoke to them on social subjects end joined in social debates, and they supplied an authority which would otherwise be lacking. Tee Union also derived its variety of tone from the extremely complex nature of the University itself. The University consisted of some 3,000 undergraduates and a great many hundreds of professors and fellows, and so it was more like a tow a than anything else, and there was society within society, wheel within wheel, and a complexity of life which brought about the very unsettled, unhomogeneous character that was peculiar to Oxford University. No theory was advanced without

being challenged. There was no opinion which wa3 I not represented. Unanimity was never known within j its walls. The! e was always discussion about every ti thing. In the same way, their Oxford -Union' Society, it was a complete mi,..apprehensb.n to suppose \ that there were only the Liberal and Tory parties. They coul I boast of their Socialist members. Of course, many of them. bad 'not had time to rise- to any distinction but from what he knew of them, he believed many of them would one day.. Lord Wolmer then descril:ed the method of pro- cedure in the society, en I said that on certain occasions there was a great deal of cross-voting. He was much amused to see tbat. Dr. Clifford once made a speech in which he attacked considerable importance to the fact that the Oxford Union Society had voted in favour of Disestablishment by a majority of ten vote. Dr. Clifford did not realise that fcr twopence they would have voted against Disestablidruent next day— (laughter)—and that there was a great deal of cros:i- bench opinion that was always verging from one side to-the o. her, mainly according to the speaking on - the debate. He (r-.rd Wolmer) bereved speaking at the Oxford Union Society ttrred votes more than it did in most place. The object of the Society , was for young men to form opinions, sift their views. . :tad examine the ground they stood upon and, grarited a smell nucleus of either party, the bulk of the Society really belonged to the . c.-oss-bench position. The Society was a complete democracy of under-graduates. Referring to the political clubs which existed within the University, Lord Wolmer said the leading C ,n- -servatiae Club—the Canning Club—was founded by 31r. Anbern Herbert, who afterwards became arvextreme Radical—(lauehter)—and the Liberal Club—the Palmetston Club—was founded by • Lord Milner. (Laughter). A rather absurd importance was attached to the debates of the Society, because people took account of the way the voting went The SJciety was important not because of the votes but because of the speakers it brought up. As a matter of fact, m• at of the good speakers were Liberal,- but the majority of voters were Conservative. (Laughter.) He thought it could tharefore claim to be a thoroughly English institution. (Laughter.) Referring to visits of well- known politicians to the Society, Lord Wolmer said on one occasion Mr. Philip Snowden came down and made one of the most interesting speeches he (Lord Wolmer) ever heard, and perhaps the most exciting thing he ever witnessed was a duel betv.een Mr. Winston Churchill and Mr. F. E. Smith. In conclnsion Lord Wolmer said he believed that free dernocrat7c govern- ment must always be accompanied by the existence of debating societies. (Hear, hear.) They taught them to analyse their own opinions, to examine their own views, and to respect the opinions of others. (Hear, hear.) They taught them to 'present their own case with RS little offence to impartial men as possible. It taught them something of the chivalry of politice,which was such a d'stingnish'na feature of English political life. For those reasons he thought that debating societies' should be upheld, and upheld in the highest. spirit and tradition, because they made more far good in their political life than many otter organizations which were more talked about and more thought of. (Loud applause.) The PREMIER (Mr. W. IT. Stansfreld), in moving a vote of thanks to Lord Wolmer, said that one of the most honourable characteristics of Oxford was that it had always thrown itself heart and soul into all the great interests which ,whether wisely or madly, absorbed the attention of the Engliah people. As a centre of the higher education of the youth of this nation, it La I been the resort not only of the sans of the barons and rich, but also of men in bumbler circumstances of life, and it had been one of the features of Oxford that there should be no servile distinction between men of noble and humble birth as sada ; merit alone bad been the passport of the favours of the University. The Premier concluded by expressing the hope that the grandson of Lord Salisbury would follow in his steps and end as Prime Minister of England. (Applawej. Mr. E. WYNNE-JONEi (Leader of the Opposition', in feconding, said Lard Wolmer bad told them that at Oxford Mr. Gladstone was the strongest of Tories. Micht he (the Speaker) suggest that what"Mr..Giadstone learned in the Oxford Union made him a strong Liberal. (Langhter). ing emphasised the importance of the sttrly of politics—by which he did not mean the eternal war between the ins and outs of parties but those things that went to make the sum and substance of our lives' environment—Mr. Jones said he was sure the ambition of Lord Wolmer to enter the Horise of Commons was a very laudable one. If ever ha did become a member, he (the speaker), hoped he would s.tay there and never go to that other place from which no traveller returne (Lsuahter). Councillor Fuurox-Surrir (Chancellor of the Excheqner) supported. .

Mr. W. &IGTITINGALE (S., Normanton) in suppor Ling paid he hoped Lord Wolmer would get in---fapphuse)— but not for Newton. (Land laughter.) There was room for men like Lord Wolmer ; there were men whom they could do without in other pl ices. (Laughter.) He hopei Lord Wolmer would always speak his opinions fearlessly and make his mark upon history,like Gladstone,Salisbury, and John Bright, whom we should revere for ever for the part they played in humanity's battle. CHURCH AND STATE. REV. E. C. E. CARLETO'kS BILL.

The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON (Minister of Education) then introduced a Bill"to remove missconceptions as to the nature of the relatiens existing between the Church and the State." He said that Mr. Asquith professed that his chief purpose in intro- ducing the Welsh Church 13111 was to " dise.tablish " the Church in Wales, and that in compari- on with this object all others, by which he supposed he meant the Disendowment provisions, were of secondary import- ance. Very good. Bet when they come to exam'ee the Bill minutely, they found that in spite of this expressed intention, the Church in Wales would he quite ns much established after the Bill was passed as it was now. The disestabliehment proposals were re ;11y a sham—they were simply a pretext put forward to corer the Disendowment proposals wh'ch were the essence of the measure. Everybody knew that the Church iv Wales was part of the Church of Englced its members being in full commrnion with the Church of England ; and nothing that Mr. Asquith could do could prevent their being so. So that whatever bill was passed, the Church in Wales would continue to be part of the Church of England, in other words part of the Courch that, was established, and therefore itself iloractically still established. He did not say they could not impoverish the Church in Wales. Any hostile Government that was streng enough could of course do that if it wished, and that was really the object of Mr. Asquith's measure if his friends would only be straightfor yard enough te say so, (Hear' hear.l But they delighted in pretexts and pretences. He had lsnown some of the advocate.; of disestablishment to profess that they had no other intention than that of doing the Church good. (Laughter.) And it had I ,en quite edifying to listen to pions speeches about the salutary effect of the temporal loss involved in dis- endowment. Of course loss of roods and temporal affliction generally was good for all men ; but it was quite as good for onconformists as it was for Church- men—(hear. hear)—and quite as good for lawyers like Mr. Asquith and Mr. Lloyd-George as it was for other people ; and they wanted to know why those peop'e who were ready to pre,cribe this spiritual tonic for other people cast doubt upon the virtue of the medicine they recommended by never taking any of it themselves. (Laughter.) In the Bill in question they proposed to do cea.ain things to the Cnnrch by way of disestablishing her as they sale', and not a single one of those things, it was found on close inspection, had anything whatever to do a ith the Church's establishment :ani every one of them might he done and might take effect without the Church's
. -tte

establishment being affected at all. First of all, Mr. Asquith said the Bishops were not to have seats in the House of Lords. Well what had that got to do with the establishment of the Church ? In the established Church of Scotland they had nothing that corres- ponded to this position of the Bishops in the If ouse of Lords, although the Church was eat abliShed,showing clearly that the place of the Lishop3 In the House of Lords, had nothing wleatever to do with establishment ; and there was no reason in the world, if Parliament were en inclined, why the President of the Wesleyan Conference, or of the Con,gr. stational Union and the heads of other religious bodies should not have seats in the House of Lords from time to time, and if the question of the bishops' seats in the Lords came beforo the country as a question of Parliamentary Reform,- as it ought to de, aid not as a . pretext for injuring the Church, he for Gee should he quite willing to consider it on its merits. The Ter. gentleman opposed the idea that the existing riohts of patrowge or the fact that the Church was an endowed institution were bound up with estallishreent. If the fact that an institution bed got endowments made it established, then hospitals were established, then dissent itself was established ; dissent was very largalY endowed, as the returns of the Charity Com- missioners. shone i, and some of them were endowed with monev that they had not got a very satisfaetory title to. There was absolutely no difference between Dissenting endowments sal Church endowments. Perhaps it was hardly c )rrect to say that there was actually no difference ; for there were ore or two slight differences, but all in favour of the Church. And here he might rem irk upon the folly and ignorance of those who were ready to say that the State found the money. So far from the State finding .the mecca" the State rather compelled Churchmen to find their own money—the State compelled Churchmen Who built a Church to find money for the endowment, fcr otherwise it would not be permittelto be consecratet.—Allading to the question of tithes, Mr. Carletoa said he believed there were some present who thought the tithe was not an endowment; or was in some way sr otter different to ordinary voluntaty offeengs. But the builders of the •Churches in days gone by were just as anxious to provide for the: permanent seri lees of a clergyman in the district where a Church had been erected as people were now. And tithe was the easiest and often the on'y way of making such provision. He supposed his friend the member for Evesham thought it would- have been better if the people in these days had given Railway Stock. Well, they didn't. They didn't giro Consols—they didn't even give gas shares. (Laughter) But they did what they could, they gave tithe. And it was a mercy they did. If what tbey gave had been property easily convertible into cash, every penny of it would have disappeared at the time of the Common- wealth. Tithe was simply a charge upon land verY similar to chief rent. It was in no sense a tax—it sraa a property. Mr. Asquith lumped the tithes and the lands belonging to the Church together, and Isid his hands upon them all, just as his friends had laid their hands upon the schools, certainly in. intention and te some extent in fact, just as they would lay their bands upon private property the publican's for instance, at" other private property, at their discretion, though no dortilt beating a re:rent, just now held in check, he sappos,d, by the dread of a general election. In conclusion Mr. Carleton said all religious bodies ia this country were now exactly on the same footing se regarded the lawfulners of their creed and wershiP-- the result of the legislation infavour ef toleration. The first Toleration Act was passel in ICS9, at a time when the Churoh's ascendency in the country was para- mount, and in a Parliament consisting solely of Church- men, passing both houses without difficulty and with very slight discussion. These Acts had made ell religious bodies equal in the eye of the law they were ail legal none of them under proscription. And as being allowed IV law and protected by law, they were estatlished hY law ; as that was the only true meaning that could be given to the term—a meaning that was given to it by the great Lord Mansfield in his speech in the house of Lords in 1767, in the case of the Sheriff of Londoc—a view that was subsequently endorsed by Speaker Qnslow. Hence there was en anachronism in using the word as a distinguishing title in connection with any one religious body, and for that reason, and in order to obviate the misconceptions arising from such use of the word it was proposed that such use of the word in connection with the Church of England should cease, and be erased as far as possible from such public( records subsequent to ICB9 as might be thought ad i sable. Mr. J. JAR)AN (L, Burton-on-Trent), in moving that. the Bill be read three months hence, said the Opposi, tion were quite agreeable that the term " establishment ' should cease to be used and they were tl.erefore agreement with the only part of the measure whici! could be embodied in en Act. div.head: BIGGEST BATTLESHIP AFLOAT.
div.p: BIGGEST BATTLESHIP AFLOAT.

H.M.S. Neptune, -which was bunched at Portsmouth the other d iy, is the largest battleship in ihe world. She is the eighth Dreadnought, and is bigger even than her sister ships. Her displacement is 1.000 tons more than that of her three immediate predecessors, the St. Vincent, the Collingwoad, and the Rodney; and 2,350 tons more than the Dreadnought, the nameship of the class. She is 600 feet long, her turbine engines are 24,500 horsepower, and she is 4o steam 21 knots. Her bulkheads are so heavily armoured that she is practically safe from torpedoes; her armament is ten 12-inch guns in five barbettes. She is to be completed for sea within two years, by which. time she will have cost £2.000.000.

div.head: TSARITSA.
div.p: THE TSARITSA.

Alarming news has reached St. Petersburg a. sto the health of Vie Tsaritsa. Her Majesty iS reporteT to have again suffered a severe nervous shock, accompanied by convulsions, and to have finally lost consciousness. The tsaritsa is said to live in fear of attempts on Ull2 life of the young Crown P. ince, and her auxiely is seeminlly underining her health.

div.head: TAFT IN DANGER.
div.p: TAFT IN DANGER.

Mr. Taft, the United States President, is reported to have had a narrow escape from assassination at Portland, Oregon. A man who was pushing forward to photograph the President as he was entering his motor, was found to have a revolver concealed in his camera. Mr. Taft is on a 13,000 mile tour, the object of which is to unfold throughout the country his programme of legislation,

div.head: GO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
div.p: GO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
Quarterly Meeting.

Tbe quarterly meeting of the Warrington Equital.le IndustriA Society was held on Monday evening in Bold-street Wesleyan schoolroom. Mr. T. Wadsworth presided over a good attendance. The CHAIRMAN said they were pleased to show satis- factory progress all round. he sales bad amounted to £49,000 during the past quai ter —en increase of over £4,000 on the similar quarter last year. The profits were considerably less which was no doubt to be accounted for by the higher wholesale price of pro- visions in the market during the past quarter: It had been a very anxious quarter to the committee. There bad also been a very satisfactory increase in the membership of 180 during the quarter, their ' total membership being 9,700. Continuing, he said that the central premises wcre almost complete and they were heginning to look something like ship-shape. In all probability they would have their next quarterly meeting in their new hall. ((fear, hear). The new bakery was now complete and he invited the members to pay a visit to it. Referring to the children's day a few weeks ago on the Football field be said that it was a complete success fr, in beginning to end. The Chairman also mentioned the recent sad accident at the Cairo-street buildings when Mr. William Taylor lost his life. He said that it was not the fault of the stores and it was a pure accident. The committee had fully considered the matter and the compensation which would be awarded would not necessitate the parents of the young man to go to law. The amount was satisfactory. He moved that the balance sheet and report be adopted. This eas seconded and after a somewhat lengthy discussion they were passed. During the discussion Mr. SEED whilst speaking on the balance sheet proceeded to more a vote of thanks to the Education Committee for the way they had made arrangements with regard to the children's day. The CHAIRMAN : Do that after the balance sheet is passed. We do not very often get votes of thanks. (Laughter.) After the discussion a vote of thanks was accorded to the Committee on the proposition of Mr. SEED seconded by Mr. FODEN. Mr. B. FARRAR replying said they should like to go one better next time. Although the Society granted 1 per cent. to the Education Committee they had not spent it all and in the future they would use the money granted them more liberally flea they had done in the past. He also expressed their indebtedness to the Football Club.

A MEMBER asked if the Committee had done anything with retard to a reading room. The CHAIRMAN replying raid that the request for a reading room had been under the consideration of the Committee, but there were certain objections to having one. One objection was the great expense width wculd be incurred for the supervision of it. Mr. SEED wanted to know when the new buildings would be complete. The CHAIRMAN said they would Le open for Christmas.

Mr. ASHWORTH asked if it wore true that any little shopkeeper had been refused butter. The CHAIRMAN: Yes. Continuing he said that they had been selling butter at a loss for some weeks and it wls unfair that the shopkeepers should buy only butter. If they bought other articles they would be willing to let the shopkeepers have shat they wanted. Mr. ATKINsON (the manager) also explained the position and said that they were losing 1:75 per week on the selling of butter. If the shopkeepers would deal entirely with them they would not object. A MEMBER asked if anything was being done to relieve the conjestion at Orford-lane and Marshhouse- lane Stores. _ . .

The CHAIRMAN replied that the matter of conjestion in various parts of the town awas under consideration, with a view to relieving it. in reply to a question by a member as to whether the contract for the fittings for the new shops had been let, the CHAIRMAN said that it bad not, but when it was it would be placed in town. Op the preposition of Mr. B. FARRAR, seconded by a MEMBER, a vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman for presiding.
