div.head: SUMMER PILGRIMAGES. CI
div.p: SUMMER PILGRIMAGES. CI
THREE CHESHIRE CASTLES - BEESTON, PECKFORTON AND CHOLMONDELEY.

England is a relic-strewn land. And under the relics lies history, layer upon layer and century upon century deep. In the course of an easy afternoon's run from Warrington the cyclist may see large wide-spreading cedars of Lebanon grown from seedlings brought from the Holy Land in the days of the Crusades, he may sit to rest in churches built from the spoils of the French wars of seven centures ago, and interview alabaster squires and knights in the armour in which they figured at the awful fight of Poictiers in 1356.

The average pilgrim, of course, has only the dimmest idea of these things, and it is to initiate him to their full inCergst that we act as his guide and administer these sugar- coated doses of history. Let us finish our interruped survey of Bees ton Castle.

div.head: BEESTON MEMORIES.
div.p: BEESTON MEMORIES.

With the more ordered society of Tudor days it might have been expected that English castles would be left to dwindle to picturesque decay. And many of them did, until there came the unheaval of the Civil War that turned almost every manor house into a fortress, and sent Englishmen back to their castles to hold them against one another.

Chester was held for the King and Nant- wich was a centre of the Parliamentarians. It was the fortune of Beeston to be a bone of contention, to be snatched by King and Parliament in turn, and once more its stones were stained with smoke and blood.

div.head: CIVIL WAR.
div.p: THE CIVIL WAR.

When the war began in 1642 the Castle was in the hands of the Royalists, but the Roundheads by some means got possession and quickly mended its walls. A garrison of three hundred were in charge and had they shown ordinary courage might have held it through the* war. But on a dark December morning Captain Sandford with eight men following him scaled the crag and climbed the walls. Captain Steel was in charge and yielded to the invaders, only stipulating that he and his men should be allowed to march unmolested to Nantwich with colours flying. It was a curious pro- cession that entered the town and joined Brereton the Parliamentary leader there. The people leaped to the conclusion that Steel was a .traitor and would have killed him in the streets (for Nantwich was a Puritan stronghold) had he not been rescued. He was tried for treachery and shot in Tinker's Croft under the shadow of the Church. His grave had been dug and they dropped his warm body into it as soon as the bullets had done their work.

The Cheshire Roundheads tried to regain the rock, but could make no impression upon the garrison. They managed however to starve the inmates pretty successfully by several months of seige. Then came Prince Rupert to the rescue and on his appearing the Roundheads retired to Nantwich. PRINCE RUPERT'S PLAYFULNESS.

In illustration of this commander's delightful freedom with English property we may mention that he put up at Beeston Hall and after having a good dinner ordered the building to be burned down. The country folks who received the order were not very willing to carry it out, and as a means of hurrying things he hanged twenty of them on the trees.

To the lady who owned the Hall he is said to have apologised, and explained that it was to keep the Puritans from getting hold of it that he had consigned it to ashes. With the disappearance of Rupert the seige began again, and a few gallant Royalists held the fortress and braved starvation and cannon balls. How long they might have held it we do not know, for the battle of Rowton Moor ended King Charles' chances, and the garrison surrendered. Yet again a small army set forth—there were only fifty-six men—with colours flying and drums beating. They had got permission to march forth and join the Royalist army if they wished, but twenty of them gave up arms and went weary to their homes. When the Roundheads entered the castle they found that the only food supply left consisted of two biscuits, a piece of turkey pie, and a live peacock and peahen. The year following Beeston Castle was dismantled and reduced to the ruin which it has ever since remained.

div.head: CASTLE AS IT IS.
div.p: THE CASTLE AS IT IS.

It is the remnant of this famous pile that we.are about to explore. In front of us, as we enter is a gently sloping sward probably the scene of many an ancient gala, when tiltinl; and other rough games amused the inmates.

By the courtesy of Lord Tollemache the site is open to visitors on four days a week (Tuesday, Thursday and Sunday are the forbidden days) and we may warider at will in every part of the big enclosure. An outer wall surrounds the lower slopes; then higher there is a line of walls and towers now nearly obliterated. It is in the next line of forts that we see the scheme of defence copied from the East by the Crusader Earl of Chester and consisting of towers and embattled walls. The Castle itself crowns the rock and here we may see all the fine ingenuity of defence. On three sides the rock rises from the valley 300 feet below and on these sides the castle is unapproachable. On the sloping side of the bill we may see at what great labour the original builders made the fort impregnable. A vast ditch or moat is cut across the solid rock and ends abruptly on the precipice at either end. This moat may have contained water and would have a drawbridge, but whether filled with water or not it is easy to see that a few men behind these towers could hold at bay the biggest arm in times when thestrongest weapon Was the bow orthe battering ram. We pass through the narrow entrance to the stronghold. The castle itself is aXwreck, but the student of old architecture can rebuild it in his mind's eye with some accuracy for there are traces of the banquet- ing hall, the chapel, living rooms and court- yard. Best preserved are the towers of the great gateway. Broken and forlorn they are still dignified in their decay and as We reflect upon the fierce storms that have beat.upon them through seven centuries, the assaults of cannon and gun shot they have sustained, the malice of men that would have pulled them down but grew tired in the effort we cannot fail in admiration of the skill of the builders who raised them.

div.head: GREAT WELL.
div.p: THE GREAT WELL.

The most interesting relic of Beeston is the wonderful well. Perched on the top of such a rock the besieged would suffer most from want of water and food. They there- fore began the slow process of piercing the stone until they foundmoisture. How many generations chipped the rock we cannot guess. but such a well is here as startles the

beholder. Through 360 feet of solid rock they went until when beneath the level of the brook, they came to the desired spring. • The reader who would take in the magnitude of the task must raise his eyes a hundredfeet above the spire of Warrington Church and then after taking in the altitude think of the patient chipping through hard rock that was needed to get below ground level to the precious water. The castle keeper lowers a lighted lamp tol the bottom and we watch the light until it dwindles to a tiny spark. There is a tradi- tion that treasure was flung into this awful depth in times of upheaval, and that long ago a trusty servant volunteered to be let 'down to the bottom. The story runs that he came back struck speechless by the horror of the depths and never spoke again. But in modern times many men have been to the bottom and cleaned out the rubbish. As a reward for their search for treasiire they found—a fox's skull. Since the Civil War little or no historic interest has attached to the Castle. It has long outlived the needs that called it into existence and its only glory is of the past. Yet it has our interest. It belongs to the age of force, and lingers in this different day, to show us how men acted under the rule of Which Wordsworth sang. The good old rule, the simple plan, That they should get who have the power, And they should keep who can. PECKFORTON CASTLE.

Our next adventure is a climb to Stanners Nab. But on the way we are to see as much as can be seen of Peckforton Castle. This fine mansion was built about a century ago by the first Lord Tollemache in imitation of a Norman Castle. It is not for small people like 'us to seek admission to the gorgeous home of the noble lord, so many of whose acres lie at our feet, but we may at least admire from outside his -.exquisite Castle. Picking our way through the tree-covered slopes of the hill we seek the crest of the Nab. Few things in England can excel the charm of the views from these hill tops. To the east the eye may range as far as Mow Cop and Congleton Edge. Northward we can see Lancashire,—Norton Castle and Frodsham rising like islands from the sea; Derbyshire hills fill the far horizon on the east, and to the west the great peaks of Wales loom large against the sky. All this and the sweet pastoral beauty and nestling village of the country at our feet make up a picture of never-to-be-forgotten beauty.

div.head: CHOLMONDELEY CASTLE.
div.p: CHOLMONDELEY CASTLE.

Our pilgrimage is not yet finished, for there remains to be seen the Castle of Cholmondeley. We descend the hill and a few miles of pleasant running brings us into the park. Of the old hall of Cholmondeley we learn that nothing remains save the chapel. This old building, defended for the King in the Civil War, and riddled through and through with round shot, was occupied by the family uttil a hundred years ago. Then there rose upon the hillside the stately embattled build- ing that is the Cholmondeley Hall of to-day.. Let the pilgrim go to see it; it is worth the journey, and he will have, to boot, miles of running through the lovely deer park that surrounds it.

The shades of night are gathering, and we join the Roman-road that leads to Beeston and home. At Beeston our wheeling ends. We are not the stuff of which record- breakers are made, and for once the snorting of engines is a not unwelcome sound. And besides why be cruel to a bicycle that has done so bravely? So we take our tickets and finish a fine journey by the convenient but unromantic medium of the railway train. A. M.

div.head: SECRET OF THE ALPS.
div.p: THE SECRET OF THE ALPS.
A New and Wonderful Medicine for Throat, Chest, and Lungs to Breathe.

In Southern Europe, particularly on the forest-clad slopes of the Alps, coughs and colds are the aston- ishing exception and not the rule. The Swiss shepherd owes his robustness to always breathing in the rich, balsamic air from the pine trees. Life and health greatly depend on the air we breathe; and it is the impure and germ laden town air that makes bronchitis and consumption such deadly perils in our midst. * * * *

In this very thought of the origin of most chest troubles has lain the secret how to set about remedy. ing them to achieve real lasting results. So called cough-mixtures are ,based on a mistaken idea; they often only succeed in giving the appearance of relief in the chest by drugging the rest of the body, which is a dangerous, and in the end, profitless habit. After all, is it not absurd to expect to put right" something wrong" with the rungs by miallowing liquid drugs into the stomach—especially when the stomach possesses no direct passage to the chest? There is no such thing as swallowing a liquid or solid—be it food or medicine—into the lungs, which are what we breathe with, not eat with. * * * *

At the same time, before science could do away with drugs—opium, morphia, laudanum, etc., which prey. mercilessly on their unhappy *victims—it had to dis- cover .some better remedy on safe and different lines. This " away-with-drugs " remedy has been found at last. In those little silver-jacketed Peps tablets we now have a new and unique medicine,free from harmful substances like opium, and one which is capable of yielding fumes that can be breathed straight down the throat and into the furthest corner of the lungs where disease germs are apt to lurk.

By the aid of the Peps tablets the benefits of the famed pine woods are virtually transported to our very homes, because each tablet is a highly concen- teated brown disc wh;sh, upon being dissolved in the mouth, releases those balsamic fumes which are breathed directly into the chest and lungs.

It is impossible to over-estimate the importance of such a discovery, for the effect of Peps is two-fold: First, they completely allay the irritittion and tickling i.e., the sub-acute inflammation of the delicate mem- brane which lines the air-pipes and lungs •, and secondly, they kill or destroy the germs of disease lodging in tissues far out of reach of liquid medicine. . .

That tickling phlegm is loosened and easily coughed up, the breathing tubes are cleared and healed, disease-germs are destroyed ; bronchitis, however old or neglected, is quietly but surely got rid of; and the lungs and chest are afforded valuable protection against, pleurisy, pneumonia, inflammation, and those other chest complaints that are the bane of our changeable weather.

* * * •* A few Peps tablets before going to sleep, and occasionally during the day, will end the most hacking cough, make one's breathing easy, and bring comfort to the chest. At the same time there is security in the freedom from dangerous and nerve depressing drugs. * * * *

Peps bring " A Pine Forest in Every Home" when one cannot think of goinr, off to the famous Alps directly that old winter cough returns, or that half- forgotten chest weakness once again asserts its grim reality. Beware of cheap and useless imitations. See the registered name" Peps" on the package before buying.
ROCHDALE LIBERALS' APPRECIATION OF MR. A. G. C. HARVEY. M.P.

The Executive of the Rochdale Liberal Association on Tuesday night passed a resolution expressing very high appreciation of Mr. Gordon Harvey's services to Liberalism, sa3ing that be has discharged his duties in the House of Commons to theirentire satisfaction, noting with grest pleasure his support of the Budget and the defence of Free Trade especially desiring to recognise his efforts for national economy, and trusting that when the time comes he will again plsoe his ser- vices at the disposal of the party.

div.head: _ FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
div.p: _ FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
THE LABOUR PARTY AND A GENERAL ELECTION.

In view of the possibility of an early General Election the political parties are hastening their preparations. The General Election of 1906 was the first one in which the Labour Party took part in anything like an organised way. The combination of Trade Unionists and Socialists which constitutes the Labour Party was formed in February, 1900, and when the General Election came in the autumn of that year the organisation had scarcely got into a definite form. At that election only two candidates who had been endorsed by the Labour Party were returned out of 15 candidates who had gone to the polls.-

THE RISE OF THE LABOUR PARTY. Between the two General Elections of 1900 and 1906, the Labour Party made enormous headway in membership and in political influence. In 1900 the total membership of the affiliated societies was 375,000, but in 1906 it had risen to 921,000. In the interval, the party had returned three new members to Parliament, and when the General Election of 1906 came, it was in a position to put 50 candidates in the field. Of these 29 were successful, and this number has, by successes at bye-elections, been increased to 33. 'THE CASE OF THE MINERS.

At the last General Election the miners, with the exception of the Lancashire and Cheshire Federation, were .outside the Labour Party, but they ran about twenty candidates, fifteen of whom were successful. As a result of a ballot of the members of the Miners' Federation taken last year, it was agreed that the whole Federation should join the Labour Party. Some little practical difficulty was in the way of carrying out that decision at once, as the miners' M.P.'s had been returned in most cases by an arrangement with the Liberals. An under- standing was arrived at to the effect that these M.P.'s should remain in their present position until the next General Election, but that they should then sign the constitution of the Labour Party and run under its endorsement as independent Labour candidates.

At the next election, therefore, all the Trade Union and I.L.P. candidates will run on the same ticket, with perhaps one or two exceptions to which I shall refer later. All the 48 Labour members (including the miners' M.P.'s) who sit in this Parliament are, with one exception, to seek re-election. In addition to these, 17 other candidates have been selected for constituencies. The miners will be running some half-a-dozen more candidates, and in quite a number of constituencies the local Labour Party is busy taking steps to put a candidate in the field. WHERE THE FIGHTS WILL BE. The 17 constituencies in which additional Labour Candidates are running are Hyde, Govan, Montrose, Wakefield, Leigh, Keighley, Holmfirth, Portsmouth, East Bristol, Huddersfield, East Manchester, Wigan, Spen Valley, Leith, Kirkdale, Crewe, and East Birmingham. So far as one can judge at present, in most of these con- stituencies there will be three-cornered con- tests. Twelve of these seats are at present held by Liberals and five by Unionists. This represents a fairly impartial attack, as the Liberals at present hold about two- thirds of the seats in Great Britain. It should be mentioned, however, that eleven of the seventeen seats have been contested previously by Labour candidates.

- Counting the Labour candidates who are definitely before constituencies, and adding the constituencies which are taking steps to adopt a Labour candidate, we arrive at the conclusion that there will very probably be not lesis than 80 candidates at the next Genera Election run under the auspices of the Labour Party. I am not going to prophecy how many will be returned, but if indications in the constituences are any reliable guide it would be safe to say that the Labour Party in the next Parliament will not fall far short of the Irish Party in numbers.

div.head: INADEQUATE ORGANISATION.
div.p: INADEQUATE ORGANISATION.

The organisation in the constituences where Labour candidates are to run is in most cases sadly deficient. In only a few of the places is there a registration agent, and of the few there are, most of them are part time or voluntary. There has been a great improvement in organisation since 1900. The National Labour Party some time ago appointed a Chief Organising Agent, and he has done much useful work and stimulated the localities into greater activity. The great hindrance to more effective organisation is the want of money. The trade unions who are responsible for candi- dates have to bear the cost of the election, and to supplement the salary paid to the elected member by the Labour Party, and this is about as much' as they can afford. The I.L.P. candidates are in a much less fortun- ate position. Unlike the trade unions, they have not the power to enforce a levy for Parliamentary purposes, but have to rely wholly on voluntary contributions. The members of the I.L.P. are also, to a very great extent, paying Parliamentary levies to their trade unions; and as members of the I.L.P. there is a constant drain upon them for the ordinary work of the party. SERIOUS RESPONSIBILITIES.

We may dismiss from our consideration the possibility that the impending judgment of the House of Lords will deprive the trade unions of the power to spend their funds on political contests and Parliamentary repre- sentation. If that should happen all our calculations will be upset, and chaos will reign where the well considered plans of the Labour party are now laid. But that decision, whatever it may be, cannot affect the I.L.P. candidates. The I.L.P. has to raise the money for its elections as best it can, and in the past the devotion of its supporters has never failed to do what was necessary. But the I.L.P. never undertook such a heavy responsibility as it has accepted for the next election. It has 13 candidates definitely fixed, and it has several more on the point of adoption. It announces that it will have 20 or 22 candidates in the field. For practically the first time it will have to defend as well as attack. Seven of its candi- dates will be seeking re-election, and the I.L.P. has a double obligation towards these men.

To fight 20 election contests in an effective way will cost £B,OOO. The Labour Party, out of its Parliamentary Fund, contributes one-fourth of the. Returning Officers' fees, which for 20 candidates will amount to about £6OO. The I.L.P. has to raise 4early £B,OOO if its 20 candidates go to the poll. The party has shown no signs so far that it realises the seriousness of the financial obligation it has undertaken. A MEAGRE RESPONSE.
We may be in the midst of an election almost immediately, and the I.L.P. with its 20 candidates seems to be as serenely indifferent about the election expenses as if

it had only to whistle when it wanted the money. The last Conference passed a resolu- tion asking every member of the I.L.P. to pay a levy of one shilling to the Parlia- mentary Fund, I am informed that this levy, which ought to have realised £2,000 has brought in less than £4OO. The reason for this is not that the members cannot afford to pay the levy, nor that they are unwilling to pay. The simple fact is that the members do not realize the importance and seriousness of the matter. If two-thirds of its twenty candidates have to withdraw on the eve of the poll for the lack of funds, the party may be brought to realize the need of a sounder economic basis. MESSRS. BURT AND FENWICK.

I referred to the possibility of two of the miners' M.P.'s not subscribing to the Labour Party's constitution. It is well known that Mr. Burt and his colleague Mr. Fenwick are strongly opposed to a change. Mr. Fenwick is a comparatively young man, and not too old to adapt himself to new conditions. From many points of view the case of Mr. Burt appeals to one's sympathies. He was the first Labour member to enter the House of Commons. For forty years he has faithfully represented his fellow workmen, and by his nobility of character and his sterling honesty he has compelled universal respect, and won the affections of all who have been brought into personal touch with him. He, as a pioneer of Labour representation, has by his work and character, raised the whole status of Labour in popular estimation, and it would ill become those who have reaped the harvest of his work to seek to coerce or force him in his latter years into a course of action his judgment and conscience cannot approve. The Labour Party would honour itself by respecting Thomas Burt. -

Councillor WILKINSON moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Finance Committee. Councillor BIRTLES seconded. Alderman BENNETT drew the attention of the Council to the following minutes of the committee :—" lath September. The Borough Surveyor reported upon the prosposed purchase of Cherry House. Church-street, and at was decided that the Town Hall, Parks and flatbs and Museum Committee be approached with a view to their acquiring the property."—" 27th September. The Town Hall, Parks, and Baths Committees having reported against the purchase of Cherry House, it was resolved that the matter be referred to 1131 General Purposes Committee. "An offer-of premises in Leigh. street recently occupied by Messrs. Thomas Sutton end Sons were not entertained." Alderman Bennett spoke at length on the question. He said he thought they were makiug a mistake in regard to both matters. Owing to the public spirit of two ladies They had an opportunity of acquiring a very valuable piece of free- hold land ends good and well-built house in Church-street at a price which seemed to him to be ridiculously cheap. He had long been a strong believer in the municipality obtaining all the land it could within its own area if it could be got on anything like equitable terms. He had been strengthened in that opinion by what he had seen during his recent Visit to Germany. In several German towns it was the settled policy for the Corporation to acquire all the land it could at a reasonable price and the towns were immensely progressive and wealthy. It was madness to throw away land which came into the possession of the Corporation when it could be developed with artistic foresight and a regard to the future possibilities and needs of the town. However, he would leave the question of Cherry House, as the General Purposes Committee had decided that the offer of the Misses Woods be not entertained. With regard to Messrs. Sutton's premises, he was not prepared to discuss the actual price, buthaviag regard to the future needs of the town be thought it was a foolish policy not to acquire the premises. It was not too late to acquire them now. He moved as an amendment that that portion of the minutes be referred back for further consideration. Councillor BIR'TLES in seconding, said the Corpora- tion baatot set an example in developing the property It bad already acquired. He particularly referred to buildings in Sankey-street which should have been set back but which remained just as they were many years ago. He was in favour of acquiring the property offered by Messrs. Sutton. It might be utilized when they came to enlarge the Town .Hall or to build fresh premises for the accommodation of the staff. • Councillor ROBERTS supported the purchase of pro- perty by a Corporation in the centre of its own borough if anything like a reasonable price could be am...raged. It was an extremely good asset, because of future possibilities. The town of Warringten was bound to grow more rapidly in the future than it bad done in the past and the value of property would be enhanced. (Hear, bear). As one who had paid through the nose for property which had had to be acquired in connec- tion with the development of works in this town, he strongly advised the Council to change the policy which had charactised it during the. last few years of only considering the immedi- ate circumstances of the moment and try to look ahead. Councillor PEMBERTON said he should oppose the amendment. The Corporation had largely bought rag and bob-tail property. Three-quarters of the property the Corporation had bought was at the present day bringing in no reverine. If they went on buying property as proposed, the borough debt, instead of being £1,250,000 would be £5,250,000, and the rates would be such that no manufacturers dare come here. Some towns in Lancashire were so heavily rated that they had stopped growing and it would he the same in War- rington if they kept increasing the rates. Councillor Pemberton was proceeding to allude to Germany when Councillor ROBERTS said "You should go there. You would have your eyes opened." Councillor PEMBERTON replied that he had not seen anything to beat old England .yet. The most recent improvements in Germany were in the new towns.

Bolton hal his way, he would spoil oven that little spot. Councillor Lora) said there were already too many places to play on in that neighbourhood. They could not put an open space at the end of every row of houses. He would have supported the purchase in question if be could have seen any good purpose to which the property could be put. IVhy not utilise the laud they had already acquired,beforo paying for more? _ _

to do their best to prevent the opportunity seine day of carrying out a broad and public-spirited improvement. The inconsistency and shame of it was that they were doing it in defiance of their own bye-laws. Councillor BARTON: We cannot see what benefit we would reap by keeping a narrow slip or land bounded on each side by property. The minutes of the committee were approved. Upon the minutes of the General Purposes Committee coming up for confirmation, Councillor ROBERTS took the opportunity of replying to Councillor Pemberton by moving that the following minute be referred back for further consideration : "That the offer of the Misses Woods, of Cherry House, Churoh-street, be not entertained." He said he did not charge Councillor Pemberton with making wilful mis-statements, but he understood him to say that the towns in Germany which Alderman Bennett referred to as being to some extent models of good planning and all that made for good municipal administration were either 'new towns or old towns, the new portions of which had been made possible and necessary by the development of certain industries. That statement was not correct. He (Councillor Roberts) did not know what part of Germany Alderman Bennett referred to, but in South Germany they had not the industrial population that there was in the North. He knew of five industrial towns of great age, all splendidly administered municipally, and in which great street improvements had taken place, and the construction of tramways and electricity works bad gone on to a marvellous extent. Those places were Cologne, Stuttgart, Dusseldorf, Vayence, and Darmstadt. Having made his statement, Councillor ROBERTS withdrew his amendment. Alderman BENNETT said be had intended to second the amendment, but be would now propose it. He dwelt further on the duty of the Corporation to look ahead and secure desirable sites. With regard to Germany the towns he referred to were ancient towns, and in every one of them a progressive municipal policy was being carried out. Councillor Locxr.ft seconded, and said the offer made to the Corporation was well worthy of consideration. As a member of the Flnince Committee he was 'greatly disappointed the committee did not carry their object. He understood the property was offered to the Corpora- tion alone and that no private individuals could acquire it under the same conditions. Councillor PEMBRRTON said in spite of what Coun- cillor Roberts said he still stuck to his contention. All the German towns were onlyimproved a 8 they improved them in England—in the new places. The great objec- tion he had to Cherry House was that the price asked was simply monstrous.

Let us attend to the-main thorOughfares-firif. Councillor LOCKER said the suggested purchase appealed to him from a commercial point of view, and he gave examples of the prices realized by property in that neighbourhood. Councillor WILKINSON said he did not oars a rap whether the Corporation bought the property or not. However, it appeared to him that it would be a good site for a children's bath and they all know that more bathing facilities were required. Alderman EttnrroN : If you buy this piece of land you will only defer the extension of the existing baths. After further discussion the amendment was lost, 10 voting for it and 14 against. The minutes were then approved. COMPLAINTS. When the minutes of the Paving and Sewerage Com- mittee came up for consideration, Councillor VERNON called attention to the proposed widening of Marsh House-lane and asked if the making of the footpaths could be undertaken at once, instead of waiting for the larger scheme to be carried out. There was a good deal of agitation about this matter. Councillor Dr. JOSEPH asked if anything was going to be done with the paving in Museum-street, which was in a most lamentable condition. It MI3 dangerous to any horse, while he (Councillor Joseph) could not go along it with his motor car as it would detach the engine. The street was a mass of holes, and at any time there might be a catastrophe. Councillor BARTON asked when the committee were gcing to deal with Lovely-lane. The roadway under the bridge near Mr. Bennett's farm was two or three feet under water on the occasion of heavy rain, while there was no footpath there nor was there any footpath opposite St. Barnabas Church. Councillor CRAIK said if those who made complaints would look at the minutes they would see the great amount of work which was being done ; so much that the contractors of Warrington were not open to take on any more contracts at present. Councillor PEMBERTON said all this discussion wasl out of order. The MAvort : That is SO. Councillor Da. JOSEPH: SO is Museum-street. (Laughter.) Councillor PEMBERTON said new gullies had been made in Lovely-lane and the flooding would not occur again. With regArd to Museum-street, that matter was in hand. He could give no answer to Councillor Vernon because it was obvious Marsh House-lane should not be discussed at present. INCREASE OF SALARY. The Museum Committee resolved that the salary of
Mr. J. McAdam be increased from £lO5 to £3lO as arranged. _ .

Alderman BOLTON, in reply, said "cheap baths" was not on the minutes, and the bowling greens were still under the committee's observation. (Laughter).

TIIE DARESBURY RESERVOIR SCHEME. TIIE AGREEMENT \\7ITH SIR GILBERT GREENALL.

At a meeting of the Water Committee, the Town Clerk reported that the agreement with Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., extending the time for the construction of the proposed reservoir at Daresbury would expire on the 31st March next, awl it was resolved that the agreement be not renewed. Alderman litNtiErr said he would like some satis- factory explanation as to why the Committee had decided cot to renew the agreement: Alderman BovroN said the agreement was made some years ago with a view to the Council securing land for a reservoir if one were deemed necessary within a specified time. That period would expire at the end of Mar ch, and the committee had now come to the con- clusion that the town did not need a reservoir. A reservoir would necessitate a big expenditure, and the committee felt they were only interfering with Sir Gilbert developing his land by continuing the agree- ment, which they did not think worth while continuing. Councillor ROBERTS moved that the resolution be referred hack for further consideration. They did not know that Sir Gilbert Greenall would refuse to renew the agreement If they knew Sir Gilbert was anxious to have absolute freedom as to the development of his estate,and he declined to renew the agreement, there was an end to the matter, but they did not know that and it would not cost anything to get to know. He (Councillor Roberts) was rather amazed at the short- sighted policy of the committe in declining to put themselves into the position of possibly utilizing at some time the agreement if the town needed another reservoir. Appleton water was splendid for boiler purposes; they bad come to the full capacity of the Appleton reservoir, which would not be capable of supplying any further serious demand, and the Corpora- tion bad the rights of a great supply which was now running into the Ship Canal and being wasted so far as they were concerned. By renewing the agreement at a small cost, the Council would be in a position of secur- ing the land necessary. for a reservoir if they found at some future time one was required. They would not be pledged to any scheme. Alderman BENNKrr in seconding said that if they could retain the option without any financial sacrifice it would be a prudent and proper thirig to do. They did not want to throw away a chance which ten or fifteen years hence might be invaluable to them. Alderman BOJ,TON said the estimated cost of a reservoir was £120,000. That meant that it would cost £250,000 to finish. They did not want that hanging over their heads, and the committee decided to let the agreement go. They had now an ample supply of water and thw did not want to incur a large additional expense unlesi they were certain that the manufacturers would repay them. Councillor Toom-; asked what the liability of tha Council would be if tbey renewed the agreement? Would any cost be incurred ? Alderman BOLTON: I understand there will be only the legal expenses that are usual in such agreements. The MAYOR : Three guineas would be the amount. Councillor PEMBERTON said the committee had con-

&tiered the scheme very carefully and they were not throwing any chance away. The agreement had been in existence for fourteen years and the last time it, expired he himself moved that it be renewed. They now found they had an ample supply of water and thtre was no necessity to renew the agreement. As a matter of fact the scheme was never required. The °est was estimated at £120,000 but if it turned out anything like the Lawson contract they would have a bill for £250,000. For many years the Water Com- mittee had not been able to mike any profit—in fact it lost year after year. Some members of the Council said these undertakings- were the finest speculations a Corporation could go in for. The funny part of it was that when they got tinder Corporation management they did not ea'n profits. Last year the water under- taking paid a dividend and immediately some members of the Council wanted to begin spending. They had one scheme brought forward to cost £BO,OOO and if some gentlemen had their way they would soon have half a million spent. It was time they rested on their oars and gave the ratepayers the benefit of the thousands of pounds which had been spent. Alderman BURTON : If the agreement is only going to cost three guineas, it would be a wise thing to keep it on.

Councillor PEMBERTON said that frith one quarter, perhaps one-eighth of the expenditure mentioned, the Appleton reservoir could be enlarged and improved so as to take all the water they wanted for the manufac- turers. The proprietors of new works would never be such fools as to build in such a position that they would have to buy water from the Corporation. Their own electricity department saved £6OO a year by taking water from the river.

Councillor ROBERTS asked whether there was any- thing in the agreement binding the Corporation o any particular scheme, except an agreement to enable them to acquire land fora scheme if they fottnd it necessary The MAYOR': It does not go beyond that. Councillor ROBERTS said Alderman Bolton had deliberately tried to put a false issue before the Council. The question was not that of a reservoir at all. Alderman BOLTON: I think we want a chairman.

The MAYOR: Councillor Roberts rose to a point of explanation. Allow me to conduct the business. Alderman BOLTON : lam only allowed to make one speech. I don't see why he should be allowed to make two or three.

The MAYOR: Ho is not making two speeches. He simply rose to a point of explanation. Alderman BOLTON : There is no explanation required. He is making a speecb. Councillor ROBERTS: I am entitled to ask the Council not to give a vote without a knowledge of what the issue is.

Alderman BOLTON : You had a chance of esplaining before. Why didn't you do it then? Councillor ROBERTS: I did explain it and you entirely misrepresented the state of the case. Alderman BOLTON : That has nothing to do with you. Councillor ROBERTS: The reservoir has nothing to do with it. The point is whether you will retain by agreement with Sir Gilbert GreenaH the opportunity you may require in a few years of acquiring land for him for purposes of a reservoir. That is the whole

Councillor BROADHURST !mid the Council would be under no obligation to construct the reservoir and he therefore thought they would be justified in renewing the agreement. The water at present supplied to manufacturers caused a great deal of corrosion in the boilers.

Councillor Dr. JOSEPH said Appleton water was entirely unlit for drinking purposes, but there would be a risk of its being consumed by workpeople if the manufacturers had not any Winwick water supplied to their works. He should oppose the Appleton water being used wept in very rare Instances where it could be under the supervision of the works authorities. Councillor ROGERS thought they would be wise in renewing the agreement. They need not buy the land unless they required it. Councillor BIRTLES took a similar view and said the Council ought to consider whether the water which at present ran to waste could be used for the benefit of Warrington. _
Coun-cillor PEMBERTON : It the agreement is renewed and we acquire the land, can we uee it for any other purpose but that of a reservoir? The TOWN CLERK: No.

div.head: CHR YSAN I HEM UM SHOW.
div.p: CHR YSAN I HEM UM SHOW.

Thanks to tho good work of the Stockton Heath Garden Society, Stockton Heath is becoming noted for its chrysanthemums and a very line display of them was seen by the large cumbers who vinited the 4th annual show on Saturday last, held in the Institute, Victoria Square. -One-of the notable features tthe exhibition was the display of art sketches from nature, which had been executed by junior members of the Beautiful Warrington Society. ,Exhibits of autumn fruit end pressed leaves were als3 shown by Mr. Dunlop, the assistant curator at the Museum. while Mrs. Hutchins, of Manchester, displayed a number of skeletouized leaves. _ _
Durirg the afternocn and evening the garden society's band played selections in an extremely creditable mtimwr. - - -

Mrs.H. V. Pigot declared the show open and the opening ceremony was presided over by Mr. Charles Plinston who was Euppu rte I ou the platform by a num- ber of ladies and gentlemen. The Chairman said that for various reasons their. President and Vice-presidents could not be present with them that day. That was the 4th Chrysanthemum Show in connection with the Stockton Heath Garden Society. It did not compare qu to favourably suth the last year's, but that was not their fault, it was the fault of the weather. Those who w.re growing chrysanthemums knew that rawly of the plants were only in bud and the flowers that had come out had great difficulty in doing so. One scarcely could credit that they could have been grown in the open. Referring to the junior section, he said it was only just in its infancy, but it was a very pi omising infant and showed sigt s of rapid growth. Meserg. Dunlop and IVilcotkson were to be highly praised for the manner in which they had instructed the children in the summer months. _ _ _ _

Mrs. Pigot thanktd the Committee for giving her that opportunity of nieetir.g her old Stockton liea.h friends, as it was the greatest pleasure to come amongst them again. She congratulated the Society on the progress it had made, and offered her best wishes for its future. She was glad that there was a sJierne on foot for encouraging the children to a love of flowers. (Applause). Mr W. 11. Woodcock proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. Pigot. He said thit during the summer that bad just closed, the children had been under the very able leader:bip of Mr. Wilcockson and Mr. Dunlop. They h, d taken the children several walks, in which various plants Lad been explained, and they had taught them as many details as was possible kir the cbild.en to understand. The children had also been encouraged to take notes of what they had seen, and thereby place them on permanent record. They were hoping that the section, which now numLerei something like SO members, would be very largely increased. During the winter they were'going to have two or three lectures. There was also an idea that the children should collect and keep plants, and also be encouraged to draw plants. The membership of the society was 750, including E 0 juveniles, but they would nnt feel satisfied until they had a thousand members. Concluding, he raid that the society realised how much they owed to Mr. and Mrs. Pigot. (Applause), _ . _ _
The Rev...iames.Collins seconded and the vote ices accorded. • _ _
Mr. White moved a vote of thanks to the judges, Messrs. Poulton and Parkinson, which was seconded by Mr. Lawrence and carried..

div.head: EARLESTOITI AND NEWTON,
div.p: EARLESTOITI AND NEWTON,
EARLESTOWN YOUTH'S DEATH.

An inquest as held -in Liverpool. en Saturday, on the body of Thoalas Frederick Hughes (i 7 apprentice wheelwright, %Niro had I ()en employed ut the railv-av ' weg.on works at Ear7estown,9nd who lived in Prince's.-, .street, Earlestown. o.n the 6th of last month he went to a circular saw at the vorks to cut some wood. A man was putting a piece of wood through the saw, and whilst Hughes as waiting the wood flew up and struck him on the head. He was medically treated, and after a few cla,s he recovered. He went out ard played foot- ball. Some. days later he felt unwell again, and he was sent to the -Royal Infirmary, Liverpool, where he died en Wednesday. A post-mortem examination disclosed the causeof death as meningitis, due to a fiactured skull.—The jury. returned a verdict of 'Accidental death."

div.head: SIR b. GAMBLES RETIREMENT.
div.p: SIR b. GAMBLES RETIREMENT.

Sr David Gamble, Bait, who has been a member of the St. Helens Town Council for two years, announces that he is retiting from the Council. His term of office expires next month. Some weeks ago the Latour party announced a candidate in opposition to Sir David. Since that time the ConsPrvetives have been pressing Sir David to agree to certAin of their proposals, but he declined to fall in with their wisher. The Conservative party had approached Mr. J. A. Baron, and asked him to become tte Consercativescandieate in oppositicn to Mr. E. Blease, the Labour candid Ate.
CONSERVATIVE DEMONSTRATION. LORD _WOLMERAPROPHECY.•
Tbe nticipatcd general election is causing consider- able activity in the St. Helens district, and on Saturday a Cons( rvative denmstration in Shetdley Park uas %Nell attended.

"Bt fore wily months have paq-sed in the new year," declared Mr. g',s, Swift, the candidhte for St. Helens, "we shall have been through the most momentous politi- cal fight which the people of this country have ever been culled upon to face. _ "There is only one issue," the speaker went on, "and that is Sozialism against Tariff Reform. Money must be raised by the Government, and by fair means cr foul they pre going to take it out of the pecple of this country. We say they ought to tax the fcreigner, and not our own people." - Viscount Wolmf-r, the candidate for the Newton Division, declared that the House of Lords wc,uld reject the Finance Bill. "We have had much to thank the House of Lords for," he said, "but the House.of Lords Ivis never done a greater service than it will do if it insists that the Government shall put this matter of the Eudget to the arbitrament of the people. "The House of Lords will submit it to the people for three melons. In the first place the Government have no mandate for the Budget; in the second place the Budget can only be defended by the pr inciples of the rat.kest Socialism; end in the third place, the House of Lords believe that if it were allowed to pass it would be accompanied by the most disastrons results to industry."

div.head: AFTER THE FOOTBALL MATCH.
div.p: AFTER THE FOOTBALL MATCH.

William Beddows (34), bottlemaker, 32, Higher Parr- street, St. Helens, was discovered cn Sunday, at noon, lying dead on the floor of his bedroom with his mouth burned with carbolic acid and a bottle of carbolic on the window. Beddows wes a s;ngle men, and for ten veers he had lodged at the above address. Owing to keenness in the tottle trade Bedciews bad not been able to work regularly for close on to years. He was in his usual health on Saturday, and attended a football match. At half-past ten at night he was seen by a man named Bradshaw, mho said, "Hello, Billy, how are you doing ?" Beddows was under the influence of drink, and replied, "All right, but you will never see me any more." He had supper end went to bed. Nothing more was seen of him until Sunday dinner-time, when he was found dead on the bedroom floor.

(Ma) On Saturday evening last at the above Lodge a pre- sentation of an interesting character was made to P.G Thomas Stanley Garnett who recently completed his term of office.' having passed through .the various offices of the lodge. There was a good attendance of members and visiting brethren. N.G. Henry G. Flood occupied the chair being supported by Lodge G.M. Thomas Seed and V.G. Broadhurst. There were also present Deputy District G.M. Thomas Forbes, P.P.G.M. Ellis R. Clare, P.G.A. Cotterill (treasurer), P.P.G.1111. Alban Boyle (secretary) and others. Lodge G.M. Seed having been asked to make the presentation said it gave him great pleasure to liresent the Past • Officers Certificate to P.G. Garnett, and he could truly sny that the recipient had done his . duty thoroughly to the Lodge. He hoped he would be spared long and enjoy good health and continue to interest himself in Oddfellowship, and intimately 'qualify for higher honours connected with the Order.—P.C. Garnett, in acknowledging, said he could assure the brethren that he was very thankful to receive that emblem, and also for the kind remarks which hed been made with regard to his -services to the Lodge. It had been an educa- tion to him in going throuo the chairs connected with the offices it had been his privilege to hold, and if at any time in the, future he could be of use in fmthering the interest of the Olive Pranch Lodge he would always he'll-Ming to do so •

div.head: INFIRIVIARY CONCERT.
div.p: THE INFIRIVIARY CONCERT.

The 'annual ccncert organised for the benefit of the Infirmary by the Workingmen's Committee of Which Mr. F. Short is now the honorary secretary was given on Saturday evening and the nrunerores audience who Rather ed to listen to it testified to the popularity of the Hospital as an object of public sympathy and support.. There was, as there always is at these corcerts, a fine miscellaneous programme offering to the frequenter of the cencert-room quite a surfeit of good things. Mr. Dee n's orchestra again did yecnran's service in. giving a substantial foundation to the evening's entertainment witlra number of instrumental items of a varied and interesting character. It is, however, a great pity that the Landsmen someeirnes play as they did on this ceca- sic nin so -slack and perfunctory a mariner. Althotgh 'several of the pieces were well within the executant capacity of the forces over which the conductor holds sway, we do not remember—looking back over a long series Of yet rs— to have heard so much gocd music spelled for went of that vigorous unity of purpcse witeout which all orchestral music is felt to be flat. stale and unp:ofitable. It is due to other sections of the bandsmen to say that the fault to which we are alluding is chiefly noticeable in the strings' and this is the more to be regretted as numerically the stringed instruments of Mr.Drawn's orchestra are strong enough. Having said so much it may be frankly admitted that in some of the movements in the suite " F.ural Scenes " (Matt), and in portions of other pieces one -got a glimpse of the hand's admirable and latent possibilities and we live in hopes of discovering in the near future that a higher standard of playing is being both attempted end attained. The singing of the several vocalists was on the whole very good. - Our lccal contralto 'rtliis Jennie Armstrong sang Stephen Adams's "Valley by the sea" with sympathetic taste, and in its interpretation her very agreeabie voice, her excellent intenatien, and her clear enunciation were points that could net he over- looked. The song "The Deathless Army" did not suit her at all, and one wonders why the rendering of a song of this kind is not left altogether to male voices just as we hold that "Annie Laurie" (sung by Miss Armstrong in response to an encore) shou!cl le. Madame Rethbone was at her best in "The Swallows" (Cowen) which she sang most seeetly and expressively. But in Tosti's Good-bye" she scarcely rose to the full occasion of the emotional climax which is, of course, the crucial point in all interpretations of this fine song. Theeenor Mr. J. W. Cottrell sang with an ease and an evident determination to throw himself into the spirit of his work which were deserving of all praise and gained for him in "Roses" (Adonis) and "My dreams" (Tosti) warm and Ix-ell-deserved applause. With the singing of Mr. 4. B. Poole a local baritone we were greatly disappointed, and it was clear that for some unexplained reason he was unahle to do hin:self justice, for, ordinarily, in such a scng as Mattel's "Oh : hear the wild winds blow," he is quite at home and can give an excellent account of himself. The violin solos by Mr. Bradford Barton served to show the great progress this young virtuoso has recently made under the tuition of the principals of the Men- cheater College. All that he did was marked by a neatness of execution and an all-rcund facility of technique which is altogether admirable, and what r.hould now be Mr. Barton's aim is the attainment Of that deeper emotional stele which is perhaps more then ever a matter of time and xi hich must wait the .maturing of Lis ph3sical powers. Mr. Barton's performances were reeted with enthusiastic applause. Mr. Foclen Williams made his debut before Warrington audiences in the capacity of an " entertainer," though his excellent work as the stage manager in the Musical Society's ar.nual operas is already well known in the town. In some humorous and sketchy songs—most of which we believe are entirely original—Mr. Williams may be truthfully said- to have " entertained " the audience ; frequent bursts of the heartiest laughter greeting his inimitable ' miqicry and genial satire. Diiiiriug the interval in the concert programme Alder- man BURTON (chairman of the Workingmen's Infirmary Committee), addressing the audience, said he bad been requested to state that that was the 21st year that Mr. Down's excellent band had taken part in these concerts, and he felt that he would only be giving expression to the feelings of all present when be said that they appreciated to the full the valu- able services the orchestra bed rendered during this long interval. (Applause.) The late Mr. I'. J. Down, a gentleman whom they all held in the highest estr ere, died in 1901, but Warrington was fortunate in finding a sabstitute in his son, Mr. Arthur Down, whose services they equally appreciated, and who, they hoped, might be spared for many years to conduct the orchestra. He proposed that a hearty vote of thanks he given to Mr. Doen and his band for their valuable services. (Applause.) Mr. GEORGE WALKER seconded and said that it was a pleasure and a gratifkation to them all to have had the services of the band for so many years. They were very mud' indebted to its ccnductor and to each and all of the members.

The motion was heartily agreed to and, in reply, Mr. Dow's, who was received with loud applaure, said he was very grateful for the kind manner in which what had been said had been rect-ived. It had always been hFs father's pleasure, as it was his, to-assist all good ca.uses,- and in that desire the band had participated. They asked for no better reward than to know that their services-were appreciated, and evidence of that fact had been given that evening. (Applause)

div.head: SEQUEL TO A BREWERY ACCIDENT.
div.p: SEQUEL TO A BREWERY ACCIDENT.
Stockton Heath Workman Obtains Compensation.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, before Deputy-Judge A. H 3 slop-Maxwell, Joseph Starkey, 24, Gask ell-street, Stockton lit ath, brought a claim/Under the Workmen's Compensation Act, against Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., Wilderspool Brewery, in respect of injuries :sustained on November 19th, 1908. Mr. Adshead Elliott, barrister, Manchester (instructed by Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, Warrington), appeared for the applicant, Mr. Oppenheim (Messrs.-Vaudrey, Oppenbeim and Mellor, of Manchester), for the respondents, and Mr. Wingate Saul, barrister, Manchester (instructed by Messrs. Chapman and Brooks' Manchester), for Messrs. C. W. Davenport and Co., builders, Stockton Heath, whol were third parties in the case. Mr. Elliott said the claim was for weekly compensa- tion in respect of an accident which happeired to the applicant on November 191 h, 1908. The circumstances of the accident were not disputed by the respcndents, neither were the wags nor incapacity. On the date in question, applicant, who was employed as a labourer by Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., had to cross the yard. to the malt, mill, and while doing so he stumbled over a long girder which bad been left negligently by somebody, and very badly injured his knee. The only answer sled by the respondents in the "case was that the injury was caused under circumstances creating legal liability en a person other than the respondents— Messrs. C. W. Davenport and Co., builders—and that. applicant had taken proceedings against that person and recovered damages from him. The liability of Messrs. Davenport would not arise in the proceedings that day. As a matter of fact, .Messrs. Davenport were carrying Gut building operations for Messrs. Greenall and the girder bud been left there by their men. The respon- dents intended claiming indemnity from Messrs. Davenport against their liability to pay. The defence raised could not therefore succeed in the Court. Under the. Compensation Act the applicant could not recover damages and compensation from both parties but could orly proceed against one. Aplicnt war in the Infirmary for seven weeks • and during that time his employers very properly paid to his wife 9s. M. weekly, being half his wages, as compensation. The payments had been continued up to the present time. About February the applicant went to see Mr. Davenport. lie told him that he was in a very bad way as the 9s. 6d, be was receiving as compensation from Messrs. Greenall was tory little with which to pay doctors' bills and keep the house going, and he asked Mr. Davenport if be could do anything for him. Nothing was suggested as to •taking proceedings( or claiming damages. Mr. Davenport said he thought be could make him a pay- ment of Gs. or is. a week but he would communicate with the Insurance Company. The inference must be drawn tht Mr. Davenport told the insurance company that the man wes receiving As. Gd. a week and that the girder had been negligently left in the yard. The insurance company would therefore sea for themselves that the man could not claim damages because he had been receiving compensation and. that Messrs. Greenall might claim icden.nity. From that moment the company went out of their nay to persuade the applicant to accept some money and he (Mr. Elliott) thought his Honour would agree that the conduct of the insurance company's representa- tive in the case was °lest reprehensible. he went to th e applicant's house in March and asked Starkey to tell him all about the accident. Obviously be wanted the information because of the threat of proceed:ngs against the compsny. The applicant told him in a very honest way the story of the accident and the insurance company's representative took it down in writing. He asked applicant to sign it, tut he refused to du so. Nothing was said about compensation. On April 20th the company's representative again visited. the applicant and said "We have put our heads together and decided to give you £lO as a free gift. There is no liability on our part." Not only that, but he did a thing which had often been condemned. He pulled ten sovereigns out of his pocket, placed them on the table and said : "There. ‘Ve are not liable but we will give you that." Appli- cant took the £lO, a receipt was read over to him, which, being an ignorant man, he did not understanc, and he signed it. No doubt, it would be the us,ual form of receipt in "full satisfaction " of the claim. TI e compensation was still paid weekly by Messrs. Greenall who only found out that the insurance com- pany had paid the man 10 when they were seeking to claim indemnity from Messrs. Davenport. Mr. Elliott stihmitted that under the circumstances it was abso- lutely futile to suggest that applicant had taken pro- ceedings against any other person and recovered damages. Knowing that the man was in receipt of compenaation the insurance company had no right to

offer him anything unless they did it for charity. Mr. Oppenheim said the respondents did not reali that they h. id a claim against Messrs. Davenport until the middle of May, when they heard that the payrnen had been made. They were taking an impartial attitudi in the present case, but they put in a de.ence to protec the third party. They would go in for the remedy elsewhe: e _ _

_ Joseph Starkey, the applicarat, gava evidence bearing out counsel's statement. He simply asked Mr. Davenport if he could give him a little relief, and did not say anything about making a claim for dr:maces. When the representa'ive of the insurance company visited him on the second occasion he said they had " knocked " their heads together and decided to give him ..1.210 as a free gift. He produced £lO in gold and witness accepted it, but he did not understand what the paper which he afterwards signed contained. In answer to Mr. Oppenheim, applicant said he did not tell Messrs. Grcenall, Whitley and Co. that he had received the money. Cross-examined by Mr. Wingate Saul, applicant said he thought Messrs. Davenport ought to pay him some- thing for their carelessness. He did not write to Messrs. Davenport about the accident and the le: ter produced was not in his handwriting. He did not know who sent it. Mr. Davenport did not tell him that he could do nothing until applicant made a final claim which ho could put before the insurance company. Applicant did net know that if he bad received compensation from Messrs. Davenport he could net claim against- Messrs. Orsenall, Whitley and Co. He did not recognize that the £lO was in settlement of his claim for damages. Mr. Clarke, a director- of Messrs. Grcenall, Whitley and Co., advised him to consult Mr. Jenkins, solicitor. Messrs. Grcenall were not paying any of his costs in the proceedings. Elizabeth -Allen Starkey, wife of the applicant, corroborated as to the £lO being given as a" free gift." George Starkey, son of the applicant, said the repre • sentative of the insurance company said: "You can- not claim from Davenport. This is merely a free gift." Mr. Elliott contended that there was not a shadow of evidence that the applicaut ever took proceedings to recover damages. Mr. Wingate Saul said he failed to see what justifica- tion there was for the howl of execration with which Mr. Elliott opened his case. The evidence showed that there was an idea ip the applicmt's mind from -the start that he had got a claim against Messrs. Davenport. There was no suggestion that Messrs. Davenport should give him anything from philanthropic motiver;-and applicant thought that firm ought to pay as a conse- quence of their carelessnesa. The £lO was received to liquidate Messrs. Davenport's liability for negligence and the representative of the insurance company only went to the house after two applications bad been made for money. The present' proceedings were • instituted by the employers to shift their liability to pay on to Messrs. Davenport's insurance company, hut in spite of this unholy alliance the applicant had not made out his Case.

Mr. Orpenheim said Messrs. Greenell were not in collusion with the applicant in any way. It would.suit them, so far as money %-as concerned, if the award was in favour of the respondents. His Honour said it sppeared to him that Mr. Daven- port must have been cognisant of the fact that 9s. Gd. was being paid to the applicant as compensation and no doubt the insurance company knew that and therefore that they were not liable for damages. He (the deputy judge), believed the applicant thought Messrs. Daven- rort were giving.him the £lO and that he never took any proceedings In the way suggested. He was therefore entitled to succeed, and these would be an avrard of 93. Gd. ner week from N6vember 19th, 1008 with costs. Mr. Oppenheim asked his Hcnour to make the order for costs against the third party (Mess's Davenport), but his Honour declined to do so.

THE DISAPPE k RING HOP.—Coratnentirg en the reduced area unclt r hops, " Farm and Hops " says : It is a moderate cahulation that each acre of hops entail an outlay, chiefly in labour, of £35 to .210, and the result of devoting the land to other crops is a serious diminution in the work provided in the hop districts. What this means to Kent may be estimated from the fact that the "hop _county " supplies no less than 4,39 acres of the grubbing up, but the tendency to decrease is the same all over the hop-growlng area, ery county showing a falling-off. How long is this process to continue? Is the ration to Le content to remain helplessly doing noti leg while an industry So important to agriculture, so ta!uable to the farm labourer, and to the poorer classes in our towns, who profit by it, is slowly strangled?
