div.head: King anti the Commons.
div.p: The King anti the Commons.

Sir,—The action of the King in sending for the leaders of both political parties indicates a crisis of no ordinary kind, but I hope the. Liberal party will not be induced to back down from the position they have taken up in the Budget. If the cabinet have made it plain to the King that they decline to have their bills mutilated in the spirit in which they are dealt with by the Lords, and that they refuse to con- tinue in office under such humiliating conditions, the position of the King justifies his action. For what does it really amount to?

If the Govenament resign then he sends for Mr. Balfour. With the present House of Commons his government could not exist for a day. Thentthe King dissolves Parliament, with what result no man can forsee. I think the chances are that the Liberals would be returned w!th a greater majority than at present, acid in this ease Mr. Balfour's government would be driven from office. The Liberals would again refuse to take office with an unreformed House of Lords. For myself I think this is not unlikely to be the position as it presents itself to His Majesty, and if so it is a responsibility he ought not to be called upon to face. But if he is trying to avert such a deadlock in his position as a Constitutional Monarch, he is acting quite within his right, and shows his tact and wisdom in the interest of the country.—Yours faithfully, F. MONKS.
24, Lancaster-road, Birkdale,

div.head: Married Women Teachers.
div.p: Married Women Teachers.

Sir,—Public interest in the Married Women Teacher's question is not yet dead. In Bradford, which rumour says is one qf the Corporations to join War- rington in legal prceeedings great interest is being taken. The facts in Bradford are the same as in War- rington and some notes of an interview which Mr. W. Claridge, the Chairman of the Old School Board, had with a representative of the "Bradford Daily Tele- graph " might be of interest to your readers. ".The extraordinary feature of the controversy, " said Mr. Claridge "is that everyone—Liberal Labour or Con- servative—that I have spoken to looks upon the action of the Committee as a blunder and an injustice and yet nothing is done to remedy the wrong." "Do you believe in married women being employed as teachers ?" Enid the representative. " That is not at present the question" said Mr. Claridge. "Many of these teachers were employed as married teachers and have served in that capacity for many years end have done magnificent service and even if the principle of non-employment of married women be accepted it was wrong to make the action retrospective.' "Would you re-instate them ?" "Certainly. lam that convinced their dismissal was a wrongful act and if so it can only be amended by re-instatement." _ _ _

It is"with the last answer I wish to deal, I consider that in one case a great injustice has been done and that is the case of the Superintendent of Cookery who was dismissed on a three months notice on a wrongful (?) act committed years ago. That act was getting married. As has been stated this lady was married at the time of her appointment and she has served in that capacity for years and has rendered magnificent service. Seeing that she was dismissed on the casting vote of the Chairman (Mr. Fulton Smith), I think the School Management Committee would be justified in re-instating her so that the matter could be considered by a larger attendance of the Committee. No doubt Mre Smith gave his casting vote simply because he felt that it was his duty to support the School Management Committee. I think he made a mistake seeing that the. attendance of the members was meagre, owing to the holidays,, and seeing that the matter was of such a serious nature to the lady in question he might have left the decision to be given by a fuller meeting. All I ask of the Committee is that they should ren- der the Superintendent of Cookery the same treatment that the other married teachers in' question had received and that they should re-instate her until the legal matter it settled.

In my opinion the Corporation has not a leg to stand on in the legal proceedings anticipated. There is no doubt that the Education Act of 1902 protected the teachers in* denominational schools from such dis- missal and therefore I consider it a gross injustice if the teachers in Council schools are subject to dismissals whilst others escape. In conclusion, I should like to inform the retiring Councillors that this question will be raised in the Municipal elections and for that reason I am pleased that the matter is not a party one. I feel sure that public opinion is on the side of justice.
Yours etc., FAIRPLAY.
Warrington, October Bth, 1908

div.head: "A Nation in Arms."
div.p: "A Nation in Arms."

Sir,—From the sting in the tail of "Anti-War's" letter last week I feel inclined to conclude that my critic is a woman. There are other probabilities also support- this conclusion. National Service has become a fashionable craze', and where fashion is there is woman also.

" Anti-War " is inclined to quarrel with me because in my criticism of the play, A nation in Arms," I expressed confidence in the capacity of the Navy to keep an invader away from our shores. lam told by my critic that the object of the Navy" is not to form a cordon round the coasts of these islands, but rather to defend the interests of the Empire and its trade routes all over the world." This may be the National Service idea of the Navy's duty, but it is not exactly the tax-payer's and it is not mine. We—that is the taxpayer and I—expect the Navy to first secure the safety of our own miserable skins, and then look after ttade routes and the Empire. If the country is in the hands of the enemy, the trade routes and the Empire can go hang. These things are, of course, important but it is our own tight little island that the Navy has first of all to secure. If it fails, then no amount of national service or rifle-shooting will count for much against the vast hordes of a continental army. _ _ _

A-mong other questions, which do not seem to me of very great moment, " Anti-War" asks : "Is not the main object of the League to insure peace by making an attack on us too risky an experiment " ? Perhaps it is. But it has always seemed to me that this object of the League is based on false premises. Let us suppose that every young man in the country has been/ trained to bear arms, should we then be immune from attack? Not a bit of it—unless our enemies were as convinced of our prowess as we. were ourselves. And experience teaches that enemies are rather self-confident folk. Mr. Townroe's Aggressors were especially so. We might all of us put up our fists (with guns in them) and ti r enemy might still come on and swamp us by sheer weight of numbers—unless the Navy barred the way. If the Navy fails to do what it is maintained for, then indeed shall we be in parlous plight. National Service won't save us; it might—no doubt would— make the way of the aggressors particularly hard, but we should all he starved out long before we could beat off the attack with our land forces. Hornets' nests are smoked out, not stirred up ! We are liable to be raided any time, but with an adequate Navy we can never be invaded. Let the Navy fail and we are at • the mercy of any first-class power. Peace! The National Service Leaguer loves to delude himself or herself with the theory that the best security for peace is to he fully prepared for war. Train every man to fight, equip him with deadly weapons, and peace is assured! That it what the N.S.L. creed aims at teaching. I cannot imagine any doctrine more fallacious or dangerous. The League is entitled to credit for its patriotic purpose in advocating an impregnable England, but when it professes also to be the missionary of peace it sails under false colours: These are supposed to be the days of enlightenment and advanced civilization; universal peace is a noble ideal sustained by the deepest thought. and highest aspirations of the best men in all nations ; national ,compulsory military service is a relic of barbarism about as much likely to promote peace as the differential calculus.-1 am yours, &C., Warrington. Oct. 6th, 1909.
E.V.W,

Sir,—l notice in your last issue the periodical vote of censure passed upon the apathy of the people for not preparing themselves for repelling an attacking military force. It is indeed pathetic to read with how much fervour we are called upon to defend "our" country and I suppose there are some dullheads who will read these impassioned pleas without a flicker of a smile creeping upon their face. Just fancy, asking me, who if I were to lose ray job now _would in about

a montfi either be starving or depending upon the generosity of others. One of the chief arguments used against the workers when demanding the vote was that they. had no stake in the country and it is these objectors who to-day are asking them to defend something which they do not possess. This class have gradually filched the country from the people until we have just enough room to walk about. Personally I cannot see why the workers should trouble themselves about a Getwan invasion. The writers I read who have visited Germany are unanimous in their impres- sions. It is admitted upon all sides that the average German is finer physically and better educated than the average Englishman. The towns are superb in com- parison to ours with wider streets, grander architecture, delightful gardens, and—No Slums ! It is also mentioned that nowhere in Germany is thereto be seen the abject poverty stalking through the street's of the towns as may be seen here. Poor people there are it is admitted, but I am given the impression that there is no class sunk so low as the poorest-of our population. Most of the towns are built upon the land which is owned by the community. I wonder how many patriotic supporters of the N.S.L. in the House of Lords would be patriotic enough to support the communal ownership of land. Who said Housing Bill ? I also wonder how many of these patriots would be willing to reinove the causes of phy.ical deteriora- tion which they so much lament. To show how lowl the standard of physique is in England I may mention that in Manchester in 1907 the percentage of rejected applicants wal72, in Newcastle 70, in Dundee 70, and in Birmingham 58. The reasons for this state of things are various: low wages, insanitary houses and towns, and adulterated food may be given as the chief causes. IVhatl want to know is why the N.S.L. does not attack those authors of disease and death, and always dangle before us the benefits of a few months away in canip which would be simply futile as a deterrent for physical degeneracy. Some of us who are keen social and political stuaents cannot see the consistency of such an attitude. Let it be understood that war is not a worker's game; it is the game of the bunking and capitalist class. The banker wants his interest for money lending, and the capitalist wants • dumping ground for the goods produced over the pur- chasing power of the people who produce them. Oh, , no! That does .not mean that, say, the people of England have produced more than they need, and want to export the. surplus. It means that their wages are so low that they cannot purchase the whole of their produce. And we have the lugubrious state of a c antuunity exporting goods-they have created although at the same time needing the same articles. Nearly all " civilised " nations have overproduction and want markets, and it is the com- petition for these markets between the capitalists of all nations that is the main cause of war. Sometimes the " foreigners " object to their country being a dumping ground. Well then we send missionaries reund to convort them to Christianity, who incidentally get a crack on the head for interference, and then .the " Daily Mail " oozes out the fact that English Men have been massacred abroad. Of course patriots could not be expected to tolerate that, we must send, an army to chastise the culprits and incidentally confiscate their possessions, establish beneficent British rule and see to the unhampered import of Brumaggem brasses and Lancashire calico. Sometimes it is the 2nlu. Maybe there are minerals in his country; so to clear him out we'll put a poll- 'tax on him, the tax collector calls for the tax and receives the same treatment as ' the missionary: Of course the British Constitution cannot stand that, and. then follows more bloodshed and annexation. The cause of war is capitalist exploitation, and at present a certain number of English people believe that the German aristocracy have designs upon the possessions of the rich here. Certainly the workers have nothing worth the Germans organising an invasion to get possession of. The cure for war is the suppression of production for private profit, and the democratic control of the forces of production • in plainer terms Socialism. Anyway, I hope the workers will refuse to harness themselves with .a new yoke. For centuries they have done the dirty work of Society, and I hope- they wi I not be led into this, the most detestable of sins, militarism.—Yours fraternally,
LABOR OINIA VINCIT

div.head: Death Certification and Cremation.
div.p: Death Certification and Cremation.

Sir, —Referring to the interesting article on" The unpopularity of Cremation," in your admirable paper recently (11th ult.) may I venture to say that amongst the reforms advocated by the late Sir Henry Thomp- son, F.R.C.S.' during his long and strenuous life in the service of humanity, were the highly.- important ones of death certification and registration. At a special meeting of the Metropolitan Counties Branch of the British Medical Association May 22nd, 1806, this distinguished surgeon showed from the returns of the Registrar General for 1892 that in England and Wales alone there were no less than 15,000 cases of death in which no inquiry was made as to the cause of decease, and no certificate of any kind obtained ; also that 25,000 additional deaths" were so inadequately certified as to be unclassifiable '— making together a class of 71 per cent. in which no evidence as to the cause of death existed. Sir Henry Thompson recommended cremation as a means for preventing premature burial, because of the dual medical examination of the body required by the regulations of the Cremation Societies. This, althoagli to a great extent a preventive, cannot be regarTed as an absolute safeguard, seeing -that cases are recorded where several doctors have been deceived, and pronounced dead a person who has afterwards recovered.

In the fourth (and last) edition of his able treatise on" Cremation," Sir Henry Thompson admits that "there is but one really trustworthy proof that death has occurred in any given instance, viz., the presence of a manifest sign of commencing decompOsition,"and he adds that "it should always be verified before- a certificate of death is signed. All medical journals now agree that under the present lax system of death certification there is danger of burial alive, and that reform is needed. That being so, whether premature burial be frequent or rare—and, from the very nature of the case, it cannot be proved either way, though judging by the narrow escapes, the dangers cannot be infinitesimal—all will agree that the people should be effectually safeguarded against any possibility of the occurrence of such terrible tragedies. This could be done by Parliament enacting the provisions contained ia the carefully prepared draft Bill of the association for the Prevention of Premature Burial, and should no longer be delayed, If any readers of the Warrington F:xamingr are interested in the prevention of prema- ture burial, should be pleased to send them litera- ture on the subject on receipt of a stamped addressed envelope. Thanking you for your kindness.—l am, Sir, Your Obedient Servant, • _ _ _ JAS. R. WILLIAMSON. _

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

Quite the best turn of its kind we have seen at the Hippodrome is that of Burley and Burley, the quaint acrobatic comedians, who foot the bill this week. Not only are they remarkable as contortionists and acrobatic tricksters, but they combine a quiet humour with their feats which is absolutely irresistible. Another popular turn i§ that of Bruce Green, the " Dame comedian, who has ere this won tame at St. Annes as a member of Canton's cosy corner troupe. Green sings some of his most popular numbers and winds up with a song and ballet dance in costume which cause roars of laughter. The Strolling Players present a novel entertainment, and one which gives great satisfaction. They consist of four vocalists in old English country costume,who stroll into the centre of a sylvan glade and proceed with vocal mirth, music, and mimicry. Some of their concerted items are very clever and reasonably well sung. The patent medicine quartette at the end brought down the house. The Strolling Players have the great merit of originality and deserve to succeed. Gracie Graham, commedienne, presents a couple of songs in which tragedy predomin- ates over comedy. They are rendered with plenty of effect, and the one about the world the flesh and the Devil makes somewhat of a hit. Other items which help to pass the time on pleasantly are given by Maude Vera, singer and dancer, Lambert and Butler, comedians and dancers and Austin and Cowan, vocal entertainers. The Palace Pictures "A Trip to Jupiter" and " The Flying Pumpkin" are unique.

div.head: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
div.p: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
Critchley—Powell.

A very pretty wedding took place at Wycliffe Church on Tuesday afternoon, when Mr. John Critchley, Lovely-lane, son of Mr. Henry Critchley, was married to Miss Emmie Powell, 280, Lovely-lane, daughter of Mr. Samuel Powell and step daughter of Mr. Thomas Gilmore. The officiating minister was the Rev. John Yonge. The bride, who was given away by her stepfather, was attired in a cream serge costume faced with moire silk, with hat to match. She carried a shower bouquet of white roses and lillies of the valley, the gift of the bridegroom. She also wore a gold bangle the gift of the bridegroom. Miss Jessie Blackstock was the bridesmaid and wore a dress of grey striped crystalline and large black picture hat. She carried a bouquet of pink roses and wore an enamel and pearl pendent, the gifts of the bridegroom. Mr. J. Herbert Hulme discharged the duties of best man. The reception was held at the home of the bride's parents. Later in the day the happy couple left for Blackpool where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride's travelling dress was a blue tweed tailor-made costume and she wore a large vieux rose hat trimmed with squirrel fur aid velvet. They were the recipients of many handsome • presents, both useful and ornamental.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. JOHN WILLIAMS.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. JOHN WILLIAMS.

We regret to announce the death of Mr. John Williams, who passed away on Monday last at his residence, Ainsworth House, Lumb Brook, Warring- ton, in his 70th year. The deceased gentleman was well-known and highly respected in Warrington and district, and for 9 great number of years was a leading provision dealer in the town, but retired from business several years ago: . In religion he was a Primitive Methodist, in politics a Liberal, and was a life-long .total abstainer. The funeral took place on Thursday at the Hill Cliff burial ground,a service being first held at the house. The Rev. J. B.,Buglass officiated. Deceased leaves a widow, two sons and two daughters to mourn his loss. The following were present at the grave- side :—Messrs. Dawson and John Williams (sons), Mr. William Crampton (son-in-law), Mr. Thomas Williams (Saughall), Mr. Edward Williams (Saughall), Mr. Benjamin Williams (Guilden Sutton), brothers; Mr. John Evans (Birkenhead), Mr. S. Manley (Sandy- croft), Mr. J. Whitley (Stockton Heath). brothers-in- law ; Mr. John Minshull (Mollington), Messrs. Albert and Edward Williams (Birkenhead), Mr. George Speed (Saughall), Messrs Joshua and Caleb Whitley (Stockton Heath) and Messrs. Fred, John, and Albert Evans (Birkenhead) nephews, who acted as bearers. Messrs. J. Bissell ,and J. Griffiths represented the Legh-street Church, Warrington where deceased worshipped, and there were also present Mr. P. P. Crampton and Mr. T. Crampton of Warrington, and Alderman Owens of Widnes. Other mourners included Mrs. Williams (widow), 3.fiss Williams and Mrs. Crampton (daughters), Mrs. Lewis of Latchford (sister); Mrs. Speed (Birkenhead), Mrs. Whitley (Stockton Heath), Mrs. Benjamin Williams (Guilden Sutton) sisters-in-law, Mrs. John Didsbury (Birken- head) and Miss Whitley (Stockton Heath), nieces. Mr. J. Hindley, of Appleton, was the undertaker.

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural Dis- trict Council was held in Bewsey Chambers on Wednes- day afternoon. Mr. R. Forsha.v presided and there were present: Messrs. A. Brooke, Dr. Murray, G. Mather, J. Backhouse, J. Ball, J. S. Sutton (clerk) Dr. Sephton (medical officer) B. S. Newcombe, (surveyor) H. H. Burnage, (assistant surveyor) F. Kertoot (inspector). . PENKETH SEWER. _ _ _

. _ Upon the subject of the cleansing of .Penketh sewer and of the liability of the Penketh .Tanning Compaoy to contribute to the cost, the Council advised the payment by the company of £lO would be an equitable arrange- ment and they recommended acceptance of that sum.

RATES. The Committee considered the estimated expenditure for the half-year ending March 31st next, and recom- mended the acceptance of the same.—The CLERK explained that the respective valuation lists for parishes awaited approval, but he lea,ned from the Clerk of the Asssessment Committee that the objections raised by colliery owners of Burtonwood agakst their assees- ments had resulted in a reduction of rateable values to the extent of £7,025. After consideration of the accounts, it was calculated that contributions of 6d. in the 2 by the parishes would be needed, but in view of available balances, calls of *l. in the 2 on assessable 'values be recommended. "he estimates amounted to £2,136 15s. For district roads .£450 was requited, secondary roads £9OO. Improvements £462, established charges £154, salaries £473, hospital accounts £67, legal expenses £2OO. The probable income was £585. On the proposition of Mr. BROOKS seconded by Dr. MURRAY the minutes were agreed to.
BAD CONDITIONS OF ROADS.
The CLERK said that it was compulsory upon Rural
Councils to take over the main roads of the County Council so desired.

Mr. BROOKS said that very shortly they were going to have the roads in very bad condition. The main road from Cadishead to Bold was in fair condition now although it was getting worse. What would it be when the winter was over?
Mr. MATUER said that the roads wore in a very bad order round Rixton.

The SURVEYOR said that the main reads were getting in a shocking condition for the simple reason that they bad had no attention for six months. This was due to the Council not having accepted he unreasonable offers of the County Council for maintenance. • lie had the authority of the County Council to repair now with- out prejudice to the agreement. This was all the business.

div.head: "THE PIRATES OF PENZANCE"
div.p: "THE PIRATES OF PENZANCE"

. This comic opera, which is one of the most popular of the wonderful Gilbert and Sullivan series, will be presented at the Parr Hall each evening next week by the opera section of the Warrington Musical Society. Judging from the excellent work done at the rehearsals the performances should be fully in keeping with the high traditions of the opera company and there is every reason to anticipate another signal success. An artistic souvenir, containing a summary of the music and story by Mr. H. Bond, and photographs of the principals by Mr. J. Parkinson, is now on sale at local music shops. The plan of reserved seats is open at Mr. R. H. Pearson's music warehouse, Bridge- street. On page Bof this issue will be found portraits of the leading characters, from photos by Mr. Parkinson'

div.head: SWIMMING GALA.
div.p: SWIMMING GALA.

The annual swimming gala in connection with the Warrington Swimming Club will take place at the Legh-street Baths on Friday evening next. The corn:- m; ttee are to be congratulated on the grand programme they have arranged. The chief event of the evening will be fhe final for the Grant Squadron Champion- ship, open to the Liverpool and District League, the finalists being Wigan and Everton. As is well-known the Wigan team are the champions of England, and Everton the champions of the Liverpool district.—A polo match between Everton, and a picked team from the other clubs in the district will also take place.— An exhibition of swimming will be given by a number of young ladies of the Liverpool Westminster Ladies' Swimming Club who have given no fewer than 30 exhibitions elsewhere. In addition there will be a race for the 150 yards championship of Warrington,the final of the Works Squadron Competition between Crosfield's and the Corporation; a 50yards Schoolboys championship, and a 25 yards race for girls under 16 years of age.
At the Close of the proc6edings the Mayoress wil distribute the prizes.

div.head: LATCHFORD WARD:
div.p: LATCHFORD WARD:

A meeting of the Liberal Committee of Latchford Ward was held in the Primitive Methodist school, Knutsford-road, on Wednesday evening, Mr. E. Wynne- Jones presiding over a gocd attendance. The follow- ing officers were elected :—Chairman, Mr. E. Wynne- Jones; general secretary, Mr. J. Walker; assistant secretaries, Messrs. W. J. Scragg and J. Adams. The forthcoming elections were discussed and it was unanimously decided to ask Mr. Thos. Hewitt, builder, to contest the ward in opposition to Councillor Wilson. An influential deputation waited upon Mr. Hewitt who promised to give his decision to the ward committee at their adjourned meeting on Wednesday next. We under- stand that Mr. Hewitt intends to stand.

ORFORD WARD. -The Liberal Committee for this Ward met in Silver- street schools on Thursday evening. Councillor Wilkinson presided and amongst those present were : Councillors Halliwell and Cunnington, Mr. Peter Peacock, and Mr. J. Howes, jun. (Liberal agent), It was unanimously decided to ask Councillor Cunninpton to allow himself to be nominated again. Councillor Cunnington thanked the Comthittee for this mark of their confidence and announced that he was prepared to contest the Ward against all ethers. TOWN HALL WARD. - -
- This Committee met last evening when the question' of contesting the seat was referred to a sub-committce.

Photo] [Tonge. THE EMPIRE SKATING RINK which is to be opened On Tuesday nelt. The new Empire Skating Rink, Winmarleigh-street, will be openek on Tuesday afternoon next at two o'clock by Lady Greenall, and in the evening at seven o'clock by Councillor Henry Roberts. The proceeds will be devoted proportionately between the Warrington Infirmary and the Nursing Association; and it is hoped that there will be large attendances. In the first place, the building, which is built of brick, is a permanent one and is die largest room in the district ; and in the second place, it is one o f the largest skating rinks in the United Kingdom, as will be readily seen when it is mentioned that it con- tains one large floor 155 ft. by 85ft. That part is for those who can skate aud for beginners there is an area of 118 ft. by IGft. on the south side of the building. There is a walk round the large floor 51t. wide with crush space at each corner. The lounge, 70ft. by 201 t., will be a great convenience. The floors are made of maple 21ins. deep. In addition, tea rooms, lavatories and cloak rooms for ladies and gentlemen are provided.. There is also a smoke room which will be much appreciated by the gentlemen. Other adjuncts of the rink are a manager's Office and skate room. The band stand is an elevated one and on an elaborate scale. In case of emergency the two exit doors and the two spacious entrances will be found to be extremely useful. A rather artistic innovation to skating rinks is several beautiful hand-paintings on the walls. The building will be well ventilated and illuminated with electric light. A slow heating apparatus will keep the atmosphere at the right temperature. No expense has been spared for the comfort of the skaters and as far as possible the work has been done by local tradesmen. The erection of the building has been in the hands -of Messrs. J. E. Wright, Garnett and Wright, architects ; Mr. Daniel Cooper, builder; steel roof, Messrs. Forshaw and Sons; heating apparatus, Messrs. S. and F. Acton ; electrie lighting, Mr. Harry Bibby; and painting, Air. F. J. Doll.
